speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And we championed workplace fairness and flexible work arrangements (FWAs), because a progressive workforce is a competitive workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These are, but some of the many policies that the Ministry have introduced to do right by our workers and ensure that #EveryWorkerMatters.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As this Parliamentary term nears its close, can the Minister share: (a) have our policies strengthened retirement adequacy; (b) have they elevated the quality of our workforce; and (c) have they built more inclusive, progressive workplaces?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, let me turn to a central problem of this generation and beyond.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They tell a story of impending workforce shortages, rising tax burdens on younger Singaporeans and economic stagnation if we do nothing now.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If we can raise this figure, we can mitigate the labour shortfall and sustain our economic dynamism.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To do so, first, we must reimagine jobs for seniors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many leave the workforce not because they want to, but because they can no longer meet physical demands or find suitable alternatives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to accelerate job redesign, incorporating assistive technologies, like exoskeletons for labour-intensive roles.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are already healthcare institutions worldwide introducing exoskeletons for healthcare assistants.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Singapore can, and should, become a hub for such innovations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can turn our vulnerability into our strength, as we have done for water.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, we must provide tailored support for senior jobseekers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have done well to develop a robust training and placement capability in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The next bound of this development would be to have one-stop dedicated training and jobs placement centres for our senior workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can establish these centres around the nation and there are good reasons to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While earning an income is clearly still important, many of them want to balance other life and care needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many of them have been in the same jobs or functions for most of their working lives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They might not know how to manoeuvre to adjacent industries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our colleagues from the Centre for Seniors have also shared that senior jobseekers do need more handholding and dedicated support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Third, unlike younger workers who very adept at searching for jobs online, seniors need dedicated retraining pathways and placement services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The National Trades Union Congress' (NTUC's) Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) has already facilitated success stories like Mr Tay, a retrenched chief operations officer, who transitioned into the healthcare sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need more of such successes and we need them at scale.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The newly-announced Tripartite Workgroup on Senior Employment must tackle not just skills redundancy, but also workplace cultural shifts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Senior-friendly human resource policies should be the norm, not the exception.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, we will also need to do more to improve our female workforce participation rates, if we are to solve our ageing workforce challenge.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Already debated extensively in this House, improving our health caregiving support is critical to helping our women workers to stay in or return to the workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our women still carry the bulk of the caregiving load.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Having a good caregiving infrastructure, including more generous childcare leave, is the foundation stone to improve our female labour force participation rates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have introduced many forms of subsidies but subsidies cannot replace the need for our women workers to care for their children when they are sick and need help.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe strongly, too, that having more women in senior and middle ranks would also improve our female labour force participation rates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It would introduce new leadership styles, ample examples for younger women to follow and change our workplaces to play to the strengths of our women workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It can introduce new ways to think and support women in their careers, especially when we need to change age-old workplace practices, probably set in place by men.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, quite aptly put across by President Obama of the United States (US) in 2019 and delivered in Singapore, and I quote him, "Now women, I just want you to know, you are not perfect.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But what I can say pretty indisputably is that you're better than us men.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I'm absolutely confident that for two years, if every nation on earth was run by women, you would see a significant improvement across the board on just about everything…living standards and outcomes." Over my career, I have had the opportunity to work for many female leaders, all of whom I hold in high regard.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: From the Singapore Police Force to the private sector and the NTUC, I had worked for female leaders who played an indispensable role in shaping my career.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They have different leadership styles, adding to and enriching the prevailing male-dominated leadership models.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Unfortunately, I was somewhat the exception rather than the norm.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many of our counterparts do not have such opportunities to work for that many female bosses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We still have too few women at the senior management levels.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The truth is also that Singapore has demonstrated measurable progress in having more women across corporate leadership structures over the past decade.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The proportion of residents outside the workforce due to familial obligations dropped to 21.5% in 2024.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As of 2024, women occupy 42% of senior management roles in mid-market businesses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This triples the 7.5% recorded in 2013 and exceeds the global average of 23.3%.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They have 34.2% female representation while our Institutions of a Public Character reported 31.5%.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) industries lag significantly, with women holding only 14.5% of C-suite positions in medium-sized firms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Human resources (HR) remains the most gender-balanced function, with 41% of HR director roles held by women, whereas operational and technical leadership roles show slower diversification.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have clearly made progress but we need to move even faster.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Gender equality in our workplaces is no longer a moral imperative, but also an economic imperative in Singapore's case.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Empowering our women and ensuring equity in compensation are all vital factors in building a productive and sustainable workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Accelerating progress requires a multi-pronged approach from various stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry share its current initiatives to promote gender equality at the workplace?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I have a few suggestions for the Ministry to consider to improve our female workforce participation rates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, it might be worthwhile for us to consider following the Norwegian way – mandating a 40% quota for women on company boards.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I have spoken to quite a few female leaders and I understand the misgivings about quotas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our female counterparts want women to be in those positions due to their own merits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, having a quota does not mean being appointed is not by merits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I think there are many meritorious women who did not get their chances because companies do not look hard enough.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: European Union (EU)-mandated 40% female board representation by 2026 has already increased women's share of board seats in France from 22% to 46%.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, we need to address the "broken rung".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Women are 21% less likely than men to receive their first managerial promotion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This creates a “broken rung” in the leadership pipeline.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To address this, we need to have companies to audit promotion metrics to identify and remedy disparities in promotion rates between the genders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Third, we need to seed and incentivise companies to introduce returnship programmes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many women leave the workforce for caregiving needs and never return because of skills and experience gaps.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to normalise career breaks through targeted recruitment messaging that values lived experience over linear career paths.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, Goldman Sachs' returnship programme explicitly welcomes applicants with more than two years away from work, reframing gaps as periods of skill diversification.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Government can provide incentives for returnships for companies that meet their diversity quota.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Fourth, we need to complement mentorship with sponsorship.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While mentorship focuses on skill building and career advice, sponsorship centres on power dynamics and advocacy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Senior leaders, often C-suite executives, and especially men need to actively champion women for promotions, high visibility projects and leadership roles.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is especially important for men to lean in because they occupy the lion's share of senior positions now.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Fifth, as a labour Member of Parliament, I would also like to encourage people to support union membership.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Unions can help to advocate for better wages, training and benefits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At least data from the US shows that a woman with a union behind her on average makes 22% more than a woman fending for herself.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Sustained progress demands moving beyond voluntary targets to structural reforms that address caregiving inequities, redefine leadership paradigms and institutionalise accountability mechanisms across all sectors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I am hopeful that the day shall come when we no longer ask about men and women leaders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But until that day comes, we shall have to ceaselessly strive for gender equality for our workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And when we can improve the senior workers and female workforce participation rates, we can have a reasonable chance at starving the silver tsunami and give rise to a new dawn of continued economic growth.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I submit that it is therefore crucial to further uplift and enhance our human resource and human capital capability and leadership in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I propose three suggestions to achieve this goal.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This will then allow us to take another step closer to benchmark with global HR standards.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, workforce transformation is critical to our economic future.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But for employers, navigating the current support landscape may feel overwhelming.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need a more integrated, holistic approach, one that focuses on three key areas.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have raised concerns before about vulnerable workers, especially older and lower-skilled individuals, from the risk of automation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While initiatives like Jobs Transformation Maps help, we must be more proactive.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What more can we do to help businesses create higher-value jobs and accessible training pathways?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With workplace fairness legislation coming, good HR practices matter more than ever.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mediation should be the first line of resolution, something I have long championed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But as I highlighted in the workplace fairness debate, some employees do not feel safe approaching HR and small businesses may not even have formal HR departments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we equip SMEs with the right HR support to mediate disputes and foster inclusive workplaces?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: HR plays a strategic role in workforce transformation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But to maximise their impact, we must invest in their professional development.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How is the Government strengthening the HR ecosystem to drive workforce transformation effectively?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By simplifying the support system and focusing on these areas, we help businesses embrace change, boost productivity and build a resilient workforce.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It appears that underemployment is a real problem for Singaporeans, especially as they age and their wages go higher.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But there are signs that this problem is spreading from the older workers to the younger workers too.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At last month's Parliamentary debate on the Workplace Fairness Bill, Minister Tan See Leng accused me of consistently looking for a smoking gun and asked me to consider there may be something that I am looking for does not exist.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To convince Singaporeans, the Minister must provide conclusive evidence and statistics to prove his point.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister has cited the low unemployment rate and increasing share of residents in professional, managerial and executive (PME) jobs to prove his point.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Respectfully, these two statistics do not necessarily support his point that underemployment is not a growing problem among Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As I majored in economic statistics and econometrics in university, I know quite well that each economic statistic has its limitations and must be applied carefully to draw conclusions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If it is not by choice, such a worker is obviously underemployed, but he does not contribute to the unemployment numbers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A professional may also be underemployed when he is over qualified for the job, based on his training and education.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, a former senior vice president of a bank who is forced to work as a Grab driver after being retrenched is seriously underemployed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But again, this does not conclusively show that there is no serious skill-related underemployment in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has said before that even though the MOM is interested in tracking skill-related underemployment, there is no internationally accepted way of doing this.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I would like to reiterate the Progress Singapore Party's (PSP's) view that this problem needs to be tracked and solved.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, we can track over time how many Singaporeans have earned lower wages, no longer have the same seniority in their jobs and have been involuntarily employed as part-time or contract workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Most labour statistics in Singapore are reported at the resident level.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The resident classification includes Singaporeans and Permanent Residents (PRs).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These statistics can therefore be distorted when the residency status of workers changes from Work Pass holder to PR.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, hypothetically, if the number of resident PMEs have increased by 200,000 from 2005 to 2020, it does not necessarily mean that Singapore residents have gained PME jobs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If there were more than 300,000 non-resident PMEs becoming PRs at the same time, 100,000 existing residents would have lost their PME jobs during that period.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In my last four years in Parliament, I have asked repeatedly for the Government to provide a breakdown of the Singaporean and PR employment data so that we can monitor the effect of changes in workers' residency status with the data.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will help us get a better understanding of issues around resident employment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do not believe that it xenophobic or nativist to ask for such statistics.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am also not seeking to divide Singaporeans by asking for these statistics.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am representing Singaporeans who want to know more.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I deeply respect the contributions of new citizens, PRs and foreign workers to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many foreign workers make the choice to uproot themselves to build a new life here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of them have chosen to sink their roots more deeply and take up PR or citizenship.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: From the bottom of my heart, I acknowledge the contribution they have made to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have said before in this House that PSP is for an open economy and society, and we recognise the need for foreign talent to complement our Singaporean core.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And in speaking up for Singaporeans, we are also speaking up for the existing PRs who are really our economic citizens.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even as we welcome new foreign workers to Singapore, we must make sure that this does not affect the interests of existing citizens and PRs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Not everyone has the resources, ability or desire to seek a better life elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For many existing citizens and PRs in Singapore, Singapore is their only home.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By being more transparent with the data, the Government can actually calm anti-foreigner sentiments and assure Singaporeans that immigration does not harm their economic interest.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will help the Government get more buy-in for its immigration policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Without the data, Singaporeans will always wonder, at the back of their head, whether immigration is really benefiting them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I hope that the officeholders will stop labelling me as a xenophobe or a racist so that we can have a rational and reasoned discussion on the impact of immigration on Singaporean workers and their wages.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By some measures, the Singaporean worker is worse off today than he was 20 years ago.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During his Budget speech, the Prime Minister said, in the past, tertiary graduates had fewer job options to choose from, with career paths revolving around a few traditional areas.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These days, the job landscape is far more diverse.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Tertiary graduates these days may have more diverse job options, but they may not be financially better off than tertiary graduates of the past.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The median starting salary of an NTC-3 graduate from the Vocational and Industrial Training Board (VITB), the predecessor of today's Institute of Technical Education (ITE), was $633 per month.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How did these starting salaries compare with housing prices?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Based on housing affordability, the median university graduate today is worse off than the median ITE graduate in the late 1970s and early 1980s.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Those years were truly the golden age for the Singaporean worker with high starting salaries, plentiful jobs and high Central Provident Fund (CPF) contribution rates of up to 50%.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our students are spending more time and money to get educated and learn skills at university today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But even after this education arms race, our university graduates are achieving salaries that allow them to buy smaller and more expensive flats than what an ITE graduate could have bought 45 years ago.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For those who do not have a university degree, the prospects are even dimmer and younger workers also face the prospects of skills-related underemployment later in their career.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans are highly skilled and educated, and they can be competitive if there is a level playing field and a government that helps them to upgrade while they are on their jobs, and not after they have lost their jobs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We want a first-world Singapore, where the Government uses its power to create incentives for businesses to keep and create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We want a first-world Singapore where workers earn a fair wage for their work, where the elderly are looked after in retirement and where younger Singaporeans feel comfortable and confident enough in the future to have children.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the first-world Singapore we should aspire to create this SG60.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the first-world Singapore that PSP will fight for.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, Singapore's continued economic success depends on our ability to transform our workforce, enhancing productivity, fostering inclusivity and equipping businesses for the future of work.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Achieving this requires a holistic and integrated approach where employers take the lead in job redesign, worker training and HR transformation to build a resilient and future-ready workforce.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is about creating high-value, meaningful jobs that drive long-term economic growth.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Employee training should not be seen as an expense but as an investment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To maximise its impact, HR professionals must play a strategic role in workforce planning.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With this in mind, how is the Government supporting HR professionals in upskilling and workforce strategy?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond training, HR professionals have raised concerns about flexible workplace arrangements, particularly regarding management resistance, productivity measurement challenges, and the need for clearer policies to ensure fairness and efficiency.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can MOM better support businesses by sharing best practices and data-driven insights to facilitate smoother adoption?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: HR professionals have also noticed an increasing trend of corporate functions, such as accounting and HR functions being offshored due to cost pressures in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The increasing offshoring of HR functions raises concerns about its long-term impact on Singapore's tripartite framework, which relies on close collaboration between employers, employees and the Government.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As HR functions become outsourced, we risk losing local expertise and influence over workforce strategies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To sustain HR's strategic role, professionals must upskill and demonstrate value.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Certification ensures competitiveness, and bodies like Institute for Human Resource Professionals (IHRP) must continually refine frameworks to stay relevant and globally aligned.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One way to reinforce HR's credibility is to make HR certification a standard requirement for practitioners.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would elevate professional standards and ensure that HR remains a core driver of organisational transformation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, for certification to be truly impactful, it must be valued and recognised by multinational enterprises (MNEs) operating in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can we build on this to further professionalise the HR sector, strengthen certification standards and position HR as a key enabler of workforce transformation?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Recently, I had a dialogue with senior HR professionals organised by IHRP.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Notably and surprisingly, the initiative they were most excited about is the Enterprise Compute Initiative.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Artificial intelligence (AI) presents vast opportunities beyond hiring, including workforce analytics, personalised training, employee engagement and mental health support.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How will the Government support AI adoption in HR to drive skills-based hiring while also enhancing workforce planning, skills development and well-being?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: HR professionals are also seeking clarity on the MOM's Career Health Framework and how it aligns with employers' organisational skills needs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How will enterprise learning objectives be harmonised with employees' career health, so that upskilling efforts benefit both businesses and workers?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Moreover, how will existing diagnostic tools, like the Human Capital Diagnostic Tool (HCDT) and iWorkHealth, be integrated to create a cohesive strategy, one that supports both organisational workforce planning and individual career health?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Workplace mental wellness must be a priority, with strong literacy across all jobs to foster a culture of support and resilience.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How will MOM ensure they are equipped with the right competencies to drive meaningful and effective mental wellness interventions?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond individual companies, Singapore must cultivate a strong pipeline of corporate leaders capable of driving innovation and thriving in the global economy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: MOM currently offers training programmes for overseas expansion, and Prime Minister Wong highlighted in his Budget speech that feedback on these initiatives has been positive.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can MOM share insights on the impact of these leadership programmes and plans to scale them further?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally, how is the Government engaging Singaporeans working abroad to leverage their global experience in leadership pathways?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim:
text: In October 2022, I filed a Parliamentary Question on whether the current slate of national public holidays was a holdover from the colonial era practice of allocating two holidays per ethnic group.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim:
text: He explained that each religious group was asked to give up a holiday each.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim:
text: His response reiterated the Government's longstanding position that the existing configuration of holidays was appropriate and that increasing them would indulge calls for a host of additional holidays, such as Lao Tzu's birthday or Women's Day.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim:
text: However, this response glosses over the important historical context for how these holidays came about in the first place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim:
text: During the colonial period, the Straits Settlements, of which Singapore was a part, allocated public holidays by ethnic group.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim:
text: This was initially limited to the Chinese New Year, Hari Raya Puasa and Thaipusam.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim:
text: But following a petition by the Malay and Indian communities to the then-Legislative Council, Hari Raya Haji and Deepavali were added.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim:
text: This means that if we accept how holidays were historically granted by ethnic group, then this original distribution of two per group would have been fair.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim:
text: But holidays were added and removed thereafter due to self-government, our merger with Malaysia and Independence, such that 16 public holidays in 1967 were no longer equally distributed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim:
text: Hari Raya Puasa was observed over two days while Hari Raya Haji and the Prophet's birthday were also holidays.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim:
text: What may be worse is that the responses by the Government appear to suggest that the holidays that have been gazetted were chosen not so much for the ethnic linkages, but for their religious significance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim:
text: If so, then the allocation of two per religion, Hari Raya Haji and Puasa, Good Friday and Christmas and the two days of Chinese New Year and Deepavali and Vesak Day may, on its face, seem fair.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim:
text: Except, of course, Vesak Day, despite being the birthday of Indian prince and ascetic sage, Siddhartha Gautama, is hardly celebrated by the local Indian community in Singapore at all, but more by Buddhists.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim:
text: In contrast, Thaipusam, despite its official non-recognition as a holiday, remains a spiritually significant and joyous affair for Hindus here.

text: To tackle this more effectively, we need to treat kickbacks as seriously as corruption.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have been calling for this for many years now.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To our migrant friends, I know you will be afraid to step forward to report the kickbacks you are forced to pay.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Again, it is this fear that makes it so difficult to detect kickbacks and ensure that justice is served.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOM has provided assurances that you will be protected and like our Nee Soon East cleaners who not only faced no repercussions for reporting the kickbacks, they also got their money back.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: You can report kickbacks by calling MOM at 6438-5122.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Jean See, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Budget 2025 will boost support for companies going through mergers and acquisitions.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Nonetheless, there must safeguards for affected workforce with acquiring and target companies.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Could the Ministry share its plans to guide companies on good practices in workforce engagement during M&As?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: How does MOM plan to develop the community of support for employers as well as those affected groups of workers?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: As the Government supports more companies to adopt AI, protection for workers, be they employees or platform workers, must be updated alongside adoption.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: On employees, Member Patrick Tay raised at last November's Sitting that AI tools that substantially assist or replace discretionary decision-making could lead to biases in hiring or promotion.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: He asked for companies to be transparent when they use such tools.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: On platform workers, I had shared with this House that platform workers are stressed by financial precarity because platform algorithms determine trip allocation, fares and incentives in ways opaque to platform workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: For instance, two platform workers who provide rides for the same route at the same timing could receive different fare amounts.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Thus, platform workers try to reduce precarity by working as many hours as needed to meet their daily earnings' threshold.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: The Minister had mentioned that the Government is closely monitoring the trend in use of AI to ensure that guidelines and regulations are adequate to protect the workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: For a start, there are three areas which need review.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Further clarity and illustrations in the Act, on who is or is not a workman, under Part IV will also be useful and instructive.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Can I ask that there be further clarity on what falls within and outside of section 18A?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This can be done either by an inclusionary or exclusionary approach, like in many statutes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Illustrations can also be incorporated in the Act and a formal set of tripartite guidelines can be issued in the interim before any statutory changes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Third, is the provision on "dismissals" under section 14.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: It, therefore, makes it difficult for employees to bring a case of unfair dismissal against the employer.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) Members of Parliament and Members who have spoken for our workers as well as our employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It has been five years since the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Against the backdrop of wars and supply chain disruptions, most countries, including Singapore, battled global inflation in recent years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For many Singaporeans, the pressures of rising cost of living were a real concern.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We managed to cushion this through targeted support for households and income growth that kept pace with, and even exceeded inflation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This means while prices have risen, our wages have increased more.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have done better than other advanced economies, such as the United Kingdom (UK), US and Japan, where real wages have stagnated or declined.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Beyond recovering, we helped workers and businesses to emerge stronger.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For working professionals in their 20s to 40s, we helped advance their careers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our Career Conversion Programmes helped 37,000 workers reskill into growth jobs over the last five years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For mature workers in their 50s onwards, we helped them stay meaningfully employed.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Part-Time Re-employment Grant helped more than 6,500 employers offer work opportunities to 50,000 mature workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, we strengthened protection for vulnerable groups and helped Singaporeans save up for retirement.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For those who lost their jobs involuntarily, we introduced the SkillsFuture Jobseeker Support Scheme to provide temporary financial support while they look for a job.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We expanded the Progressive Wage Model (PWM), we raised the Local Qualifying Salary (LQS), we enhanced the Workfare Income Supplement to boost their incomes and CPF savings.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Up to nine in 10 full-time, lower-wage workers are now covered by PWM, LQS and the Progressive Wage (PW) Mark.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For platform workers, we strengthened their housing and retirement adequacy, their work injury compensation and representation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For persons with disabilities, we boosted their employment from 28% to 34% over the past five years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: About 740,000 Singaporeans will be eligible for the enhanced Matched Retirement Savings Scheme (MRSS).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We want to assure all Singaporeans that they can meet their basic retirement needs so long as they work and contribute consistently to CPF.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also uplift those who are unable to, or lack the runway to work and save through CPF.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Third, COVID-19 was a wake-up call for businesses to drive productivity and strengthen resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We refreshed, therefore, our work pass framework to enable this.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We launched the Overseas Networks and Expertise Pass (ONE Pass) for global talent; and the COMPASS for Employment Pass (EP) holders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We remained disciplined in our reliance on Work Permit holders to spur industry transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked how successful this has been.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Since 2019, we have launched 17 Jobs Transformation Maps.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Around 10,000 companies received support to train and to hire workers, and to redesign jobs through schemes, like the Career Conversion Programmes (CCPs).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We also launched the HR Industry Transformation Plan in 2023 to drive our workforce transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We launched the Tripartite Guidelines on Flexible Work Arrangement Requests and we built employer capabilities to better attract and retain talent in the workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This initiative could potentially unlock access to a sizeable group, with about 240,000 women and 130,000 seniors of working age, which is outside the labour force today.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We passed the Workplace Fairness Bill to combat workplace discrimination.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We improved the well-being and safety of migrant workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We introduced primary care plans, we raised operating standards in dormitories, we improved service offerings at Recreation Centres and we attained a record low workplace fatality rate of 0.99 fatalities per 100,000 workers in 2023.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These achievements were only possible with the strong support of our tripartite partners, the NTUC and the Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With significant geopolitical and economic uncertainties ahead, we have projected a more cautious pace of GDP growth in 2025, at about 1% to 3%.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In the longer term, two forces will make growth even harder to sustain.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With our low fertility, our resident workforce is expected to stop growing by the next decade.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: One in four Singaporeans are projected to be aged 65 and above by 2030.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Southeast Asia will benefit from a demographic dividend and we need to keep up as the rest of Southeast Asia grows.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Cities, like New York, London and Dubai, they are attracting top companies and talent in fields like biotechnology and AI.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Amidst these challenges, how can we continually grow the economic pie?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: How do we continue to create meaningful opportunities for Singaporeans?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, we have to continue to remain open to the world to stay competitive and to support our society's needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Including them, the old age support ratio in 2024 rises from 3.5 to 5.2.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But there are limits to growing through numbers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The only sustainable way forward is through productivity-driven growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have made good progress on our productivity journey.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, even so, Singapore's productivity remains at 40% to 70% of frontier economies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There is an exciting opportunity, and that is for us to reshape our economy into one that is driven by productivity and innovation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The global order has also changed dramatically in a matter of weeks.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Singapore can stand out as a beacon of stability and as a beacon of openness, drawing in global talent, drawing in global companies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Gan shared earlier on today in his Ministry of Trade and Industry COS speech, we will strengthen our connectivity to the world; we will help our local companies build new brands and new businesses; we will foster a pro-enterprise environment for growth in areas like advanced manufacturing, deep tech and the green economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: People – their passion, ingenuity, skills – these are at the heart of this journey.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM will build a workforce that is adaptable, innovative and diverse, helping Singapore thrive in a turbulent world.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have three priorities this year: (a) enabling businesses to transform; (b) empowering workers to build career health; and (c) fostering inclusive and safe workplaces.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Businesses understand this need, but they face a high-cost environment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Part of the increase in manpower cost has been necessary to uplift our lower-wage workers, and this is a priority in our country's social compact.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will alleviate businesses' short-term pressures while we drive and continue to drive long-term transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, we will empower workers to build their career health through different life stages even as our economy transforms.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And third, we will foster fair, inclusive and safe workplaces.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It will address the calls from Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Sharael Taha, Mr Edward Chia and Ms Jean See for more holistic and integrated support for enterprise workforce transformation, with three main features.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, we will introduce a new SkillsFuture Workforce Development Grant.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This will bring together schemes administered by WSG and SSG, and simplify the application process.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Companies can access a holistic suite of workforce development support via one application channel, for activities like job redesign, capability building and training.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: WSG will work with anchor programme partners to advise companies on suitable and sustainable solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, we will enhance support for job redesign.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Currently, WSG provides funding support of up to 50%, capped at $30,000, for companies to engage pre-approved consultants on job redesign.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also review and raise the cap of $30,000.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some larger companies have begun identifying workers who may be impacted by AI and proactively reskilling them for new jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But other companies, especially SMEs, may need more support for job redesign to address disruptions like the impact of AI.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will expand the scope of coverage for job redesign expenses beyond consultancy services to include equipping line managers and HR with job redesign and change management skills in identifying workforce solutions and AI tools.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will share more details in due course.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Third, the SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit will be redesigned in 2026 to better support workforce transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We received feedback that the reimbursement model could better address companies' cash flow issues and be clearer as to which schemes the credits could be used for.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With the redesigned scheme, eligible companies will get a fresh $10,000 of credits.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Like an online wallet, companies can use the credits to offset out-of-pocket expenses on relevant workforce transformation programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The NTUC's Company Training Committee (CTC) Grant was enhanced in 2024 to support training tied to business transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As of December 2024, the CTC Grant has supported more than 400 transformation projects, benefiting over 7,000 workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Take Ms Rachel Lee, a tax advisor at BDO Tax Advisory.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Rachel used to spend many hours on manual tasks, like data collection and document preparation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Using the CTC Grant, BDO Tax Advisory introduced a centralised data platform with a smarter and faster workflow, automated data collection and validation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And this, therefore, allowed Rachel to focus on providing clients personalised support, improving business outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As announced by the Prime Minister in his Budget speech, we will set aside around $200 million to scale up the grant and to extend it to 2028.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: How can educational institutions and employers collaborate to develop future-ready employees?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Today, they can co-develop workforce training programmes customised to business needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also expand the CTC Grant to fund employer-led training that provides workers formal certifications.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The CTC Grant will provide enhanced support via course fee subsidies and absentee payroll.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We thank Mr Patrick Tay, Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Edward Chia for their suggestions to improve HR practices and standards.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Businesses have cited, continually so, manpower constraints as a key challenge.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the same time, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim shared that there is ground scepticism over the need for foreign talent.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When we see a foreigner, we think, "They are taking a job a Iocal could have had".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But what is harder to see is that, without the access to foreigners, the company and its jobs may not even be in Singapore to begin with.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The hard truth is that Singapore has a small domestic market and we have no natural resources.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As Minister Mentor Mr Lee Kuan Yew once said, "If we do not attract, we do not welcome and we do not make talent feel comfortable in Singapore, we will not be a global city, and we will not count for much." So, it is very easy to use simplistic arguments to insinuate that it is a zero-sum game, that if you remove one foreigner, you get one more job for a local.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Leong shared that he is for an open economy and open society, and asked for facts to support this, to quell anti-immigration sentiments.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I take note that he is trained in econometrics, he is a statistician.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But please do not underestimate the power of the entire team of Government economists, scholars, Government statisticians who are monitoring this for many, many years and many, many decades, and have also understood the trends.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: One in three of the increase in resident PMETs came from non-PMETs upgrading to higher-skilled PMET roles, with residents in their 30s to 50s forming the majority.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Members of the House, our upskilling programmes, our investments in our local non-PMETs to upgrade to PMETs have borne fruit.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In the Financial and Insurance Services, Professional Services and Information and Communications Technology (ICT) sectors, EP and S Pass holders increased by 18,000.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Resident PMETs increased by 172,000, again a 10-fold increase.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As of 2024, there were three to six resident PMETs for every one EP or S Pass holder in these sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The same story holds, even if one compares only Singapore Citizens, or even local-born Singapore Citizens, to EP and S Pass holders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Resident data largely mirrors citizen data, because Singapore Citizens have consistently made up about 84% of the resident workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM has periodically released statistics and analyses on the employment outcomes of Singapore Citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Employment outcomes for Singapore Citizens have been favourable over the last decade.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The labour force participation rate of Singapore Citizens has risen, making it one of the highest globally.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is ahead of cities in Japan, Finland and Germany.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The unemployment rate of Singapore Citizens has remained stable and low over the decade and, internationally, Singapore has one of the lowest unemployment rates.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We should never develop a "Singaporean only" mentality, because this would deprive us of talent needed to anchor global businesses that benefit Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Foreign-owned firms comprise less than one-quarter of companies in Singapore, but they employ about one-third of resident workers, and about 60% of residents in high-paying jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our own local enterprises have benefited from servicing multinational corporations (MNCs) and gaining global exposure.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Global companies and foreigners also pay taxes that help fund Government spending on education, healthcare and housing.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our work pass framework is carefully managed to provide access to high-quality foreigners who support productive sectors and create good jobs for locals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Miss Rachel Ong and Mr Mohd Fahmi have asked for updates on this.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Beyond economic contributions, ONE Pass holders have contributed to the local community, mentoring local leaders and startups, volunteering with social organisations and collaborating with our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Take Ms Savita Iyer, the chief financial officer for The Walt Disney Company Southeast Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: She has worked across the globe and volunteers as a mentor with the Singapore Leaders Network Fellowship Programme, which prepares Singaporeans for regional and global leadership roles.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: One of her mentees is Ms Sueann Yeo, Head of APAC Private Wealth Client Relation, EQT Group.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Ms Yeo feels empowered to have a female mentor who is a leader in her field and to apply her mentor's experience to her own leadership journey.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the EP level, we have finetuned our framework to ensure that EP holders complement our local workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The EP qualifying salary is benchmarked to the top one-third of the local PMET wages to ensure that EP holders are of high calibre.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim suggested levelling the salaries for local and foreign workers through a CPF escrow.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I believe this is unnecessary, because when setting the qualifying salary, we already include CPF contributions in the local wage benchmarks.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In salary terms, the playing field is actually quite fair.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: While the take-home pay of an EP holder may be higher because they do not contribute to CPF, this does not mean locals are paid less, because their CPF contributions go towards housing and retirement needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked for an update on how our EP framework incentivises businesses to develop a strong local core.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We implemented COMPASS about a year and a half ago.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Firms more dependent on foreigners of a single nationality or foreigners in general will have to diversify their workforce or they have to hire more locals to pass COMPASS.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the S Pass level, we will continue to raise the quality of our workforce and safeguard employment opportunities for local associate professionals and technicians (APTs).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have benchmarked the minimum cost of hiring for S Pass holders to the top one-third of local APT wages.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To ease the transition, we phased out the increase in the S Pass qualifying salary over three steps.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We announced it in 2022, and phased it out over three steps, in 2022, 2023 and 2025.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In light of businesses' cost challenges, we have moderated the increase.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For the Financial Services sector, it will be raised from $3,650 to $3,800.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Per usual, the qualifying salaries will increase with age.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These changes will apply to new S Pass applications from 1 September 2025, and renewal applications expiring from 1 September 2026.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will continue to review the S Pass qualifying salary against the benchmark, given prevailing economic conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the Work Permit level, numbers are at an all-time high, 17% above pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Sectors more reliant on Work Permit holders, such as Construction, Food Services and Accommodation, have experienced low or negative productivity growth over the last decade.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: You might have read – over 3,000 F&B outlets closed in 2024.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But these closures were outpaced by almost 4,000 new openings, with a 4% increase in Work Permit holders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As Mr Fahmi urged, businesses need to reduce reliance on Work Permit holders by raising productivity and redesigning jobs for locals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Recognising this, the Alliance for Action (AfA) on Business Competitiveness made helpful recommendations to enable businesses to hire higher-skilled workers – and go for quality over quantity.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Mark Lee asked about the recommendation to allow cross-deployment of foreign workers across sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is a complex issue – we need to balance the potential efficiencies against the risk of circumvention of our work pass controls.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Having said that, we are studying this in consultation with industry partners and will update when ready.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: On the other recommendations, we will adopt them to enhance our Work Permit framework.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, we will remove the maximum period of employment restrictions for Work Permit holders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Previously, period of employment was capped at 14 to 26 years – causing firms to let go of experienced workers who could be at prime working age.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also raise the maximum employment age of Work Permit Holders to align with the local retirement age, currently 63.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With these changes, employers can retain experienced workers who are still able to contribute.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Jayakumar has worked at KTC Civil Engineering and Construction for 25 years, joining as an Assistant Foreman before rising the ranks to Foreman.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With his wealth of experience, Mr Jayakumar mentors and trains newer workers, helps instill a strong culture of safety, and promotes best practices.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: KTC welcomes the removal of the maximum period of employment restrictions, which allows experienced workers like Mr Jayakumar to continue contributing to the company's productivity and delivery of projects.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, we will expand the list of Non-Traditional Sources to include Laos, Cambodia and Bhutan, considering industry demand.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This will allow firms to build a more skilled and resilient workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Third, we will expand the Non-Traditional Sources Occupation List (NTS-OL), to enable businesses in Services and Manufacturing to hire skilled workers from Non-Traditional Sources in more non-PMET occupations, in consultation with industry partners and unions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: On top of that, we have included nearly all the manufacturing operator roles recommended by the AfA.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also include heavy vehicle drivers and cooks.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As NTS-OL workers must be paid at least $2,000, this will not undermine efforts to uplift locals in these occupations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Manpower for Strategic Economic Priorities (M-SEP) scheme provides transitionary Work Permit and S Pass quota to firms contributing to Singapore's economic priorities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will expand the eligible programmes and add a new pathway for firms that send locals on overseas exposure or leadership programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the same time, we recognise there are essential roles that are difficult to automate and recruit locals for.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have been providing targeted flexibilities, such as for conservancy cleaning.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second Minister for Home Affairs Josephine Teo shared how the Ministry of Home Affairs is carefully augmenting the recruitment pool with foreigners for emergency medical services and auxiliary police officers, even as they maintain a strong local core.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Ms Hazel Poa also suggested allocating more foreign workforce quota to firms with inclusive employment practices.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are actively reviewing our Work Permit framework to drive transformation, while nuancing it to support different needs as our workforce changes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Singaporeans have a world-class education and work ethic.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As our economy transforms, we are well-poised to take advantage of new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The OECD's Survey of Adult Skills found that Singaporeans' literacy skills declined as early as in their mid-30s.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We must do more to pursue lifelong learning.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In our Forward Singapore engagements, Singaporeans shared that they looked forward to new opportunities but were uncertain how to get there.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Career Health SG is our commitment to empower Singaporeans to develop meaningful and resilient careers amidst economic changes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For instance, as mentioned in my Ministry of Trade and Industry COS speech, as we transition to a green economy, we are actively reskilling workers to take on new or redesigned green jobs through programmes like the CCP for Sustainability Professionals and the CCP for Future Energy and Chemical sector.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Employers also have a big part to play in supporting their employees.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: An SBF survey showed 60% of large companies and less than half of SMEs provide their employees with training.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When business is good, there is no time to train.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When business is bad, there is no money to train.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Employers may also be unsure how to guide employees in their career journey.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That is why we have invested in a holistic set of initiatives to support Singaporeans' career health.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will elaborate on MOM's efforts to empower Singaporeans to build career health and strengthen support for employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Leong Mun Wai asked about underemployment in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Leong has asserted, not for the first time, that underemployment is a severe problem – that it is increasingly difficult for Singaporeans to find jobs matching their skills and aspirations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I want to share with everyone – I understand the anxieties and I empathise with the apprehensions that Singaporeans today have, that they feel in a rapidly changing world.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As Mr Patrick Tay mentioned, the faster pace of economic transformation, all of this accelerated change may lead to mismatches between employers' needs and workers' aspirations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The underemployment that Mr Leong described earlier is referred to as skills-related underemployment, where individuals believe that their job does not fully utilise their skills.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, today, there is no internationally accepted way to measure this.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I shared before – we are working with the International Labour Organization (ILO) to develop such measurements.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But this international collaborative process will take time.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: What we have and what we can measure objectively is time-related underemployment, which he talked about – the one-hour time rate.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is well-defined and an internationally accepted measure.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This means, persons working part-time but willing and able to engage in additional work.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is lower than many other developed economies like the United Kingdom (UK) and Finland.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some workers have personal reasons for taking on jobs that may not match their qualifications – reasons like passion, lifestyle goals or caregiving needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We respect these choices and we want those who are underemployed voluntarily to have a range of jobs to choose from to suit their needs and their aspirations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The most common example, which Mr Leong also cited as proof of underemployment, are former PMETs – his example of a senior vice president of a bank who is now a private hire driver.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, we should be very careful about using anecdotal examples and extrapolating this.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Similarly, a survey by Grab shows that more than 70% of their drivers have chosen to take up this work because of "flexibility of time".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM's latest survey shows that 94.1% of SEPs who did own account work as a primary form of their livelihood, for example, financial advisors, insurance agents, real estate agents, taxi drivers, private-hire car drivers, preferred such work arrangements.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Among them are degree holders who willingly take on jobs that typically do not require a degree because either they found the current work meaningful, because it suits their needs, or maybe it gives them the flexibility that they want.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: On the other metrics that Mr Leong alluded to, the picture is also not the dire one that he has painted.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Compared to other developed economies, our residents have one of the highest median incomes and labour force participation rates, and lowest unemployment rates.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Incomes of residents have risen across all percentiles in the last decade.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Residents earn one of the highest wages in the world, unlike in many other developed countries where wages have either stagnated or declined.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The median starting salaries of our graduates are higher than other countries like the UK and Australia, even after adjusting for purchasing power parity.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This corresponds to the share of tertiary-educated workers in the resident workforce, which increased from 51% to slightly over 60%, over the same period that we are comparing.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If underemployment was widespread, the PMET share would be much lower than the share of tertiary-educated workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Majority of these were seniors, whom we are now helping to upskill them for new job opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I understand – I spend a lot of time talking about the data, but the data may not reassure those who are feeling anxious or who may have lived experiences, difficulties going through their livelihood, struggling to find roles, struggling to find purpose and meaning in life, or to find roles that match their expectations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have a wide range of programmes to help you stay up to date in the job market, for you to stay employed, for you to stay confident, for you to seize good job opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That is the spirit behind our Career Health SG.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, we have a whole list of help schemes that are available.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I put up a glossary just to help me, to remind myself as I am going through this speech.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the same time, we are committed to ensuring a fair level playing field.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will continue to promote fair employment practices and we will take firm actions against discriminatory hiring.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That is how we pass the Workplace Fairness Legislation Bill a month and a half ago.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For those facing setbacks, we have your back.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And like I said, this is just a transitional support scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It sits on top of whatever social assistance schemes that you are already on.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will share how eligible individuals can qualify for payouts under the scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For Singaporeans aspiring to become corporate leaders, overseas exposure is crucial.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Through the Forward SG exercise, the AfAs on Business Leadership Development (AfA-BLD) and on Business Competitiveness, businesses have highlighted constantly the need for Singaporean corporate leaders with global exposure and perspectives.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As stated in the Forward SG report, we will do more to help Singaporeans stand out as leaders in their respective fields.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Edward Chia will be glad to learn that we will redouble our efforts to groom the next generation of Singapore Global Leaders on three fronts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, as announced by Prime Minister in his Budget speech, we will expand career development opportunities for Singaporean professionals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Today, we support companies to groom Singaporean talents through overseas postings and leadership milestone programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This will enable us to groom homegrown leaders, like Andrew Chia, the Head of Wealth and Retail Banking for Singapore, ASEAN and South Asia at Standard Chartered Bank.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Prior to his current role, MAS supported his posting to Jakarta as CEO of Standard Chartered Bank Indonesia, as part of their International Postings Programme (iPOST).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The invaluable experience prepared him for the current role overseeing the Singaporean franchise and eight other regional markets.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, we will enhance overseas transition support for Singaporeans and their families.
