speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We know that moving overseas and back can be difficult for families, especially on housing and children's education.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Ministry of Education (MOE) has measures to support families' education needs and preferences.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Through the Assured School Placement scheme, MOE ensures that children of returning Singaporeans are guaranteed a place in a primary or secondary school with vacancies near their home.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Those seeking admission to a secondary school based on merit and choice can also take part in the School Placement Exercise for Returning Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It will connect participants with in-market communities and provide guidance on housing and education matters through relevant agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Third, we will strengthen the ecosystem of our leadership communities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These are crucial for building professional networks and accessing career resources.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong mentioned, we will enhance SGLN to provide overseas transition support.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will scale-up networking programmes, mentorship opportunities and the flagship SGLN Fellowship programme for middle to senior Singaporean managers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will share more details soon and I really encourage all aspiring Singaporean leaders to join the network.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also foster cross-sector networking between SGLN and sectoral communities, like the Singapore Financial Leaders Network and the SG Digital Leadership Accelerator.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As our population ages, we need to really be very forward-leaning on extending the productive longevity of seniors and strengthening retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, we will help our senior workers to remain productive for as long as they wish to.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will launch a tripartite-led effort this year to co-develop ideas with citizens and businesses on enabling multi-stage careers for mature workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also, at the same time, extend the CPF Transition Offset for employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim suggested changes to the CPF system, including increasing the amount that members can withdraw at age 55.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I think she knows that this will reduce members' future monthly payouts when they might need it most.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The current withdrawal rules strike a balance between members' immediate needs and ensuring sufficient retirement income for life.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Property owners have the flexibility to set aside their Full Retirement Sum in property and cash to withdraw their retirement account savings above the Basic Retirement Sum.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And members born from 1958 can also withdraw up to 20% of their retirement account savings when they turn 65.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To Ms Sylvia Lim's other suggestion to require spousal consent for CPF nominations, our current approach, I have said that before, is aligned with that for wills.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The distribution of one's assets is a personal decision.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Requiring spousal consent would mean members are no longer free to choose who would receive their CPF savings upon their demise.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will continue reviewing our CPF policies to ensure relevance.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have made good progress in strengthening the retirement adequacy for Singaporeans through moves in the last two years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have also put up the Majulah Package where 1.6 million Singaporeans received the MediSave bonus in December 2024 and about 800,000 also received the Retirement Savings Bonus.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: From this year, eligible working seniors will receive the annual Earn and Save Bonus for as long as they work.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And this is how the Government has enhanced Singaporeans' retirement adequacy, even as we study moves, such as the Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme, which Mr Louis Chua mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will share more on our initiatives to help seniors build their retirement savings and stay engaged in the workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is also important that we foster fair and inclusive workplaces, so that all workers can share in the fruits of our growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will continue to uplift our lower-wage workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To help them upskill for better jobs, we will enhance Workfare Skill Support.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also enhance the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme (PWCS) to support employers in wage increases.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad will share more.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We want to foster inclusive workplaces where everyone can contribute, even with different work arrangements.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will enhance CCPs for the reskilling of mid-career new hires and employees on flexi-load jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For persons with disabilities, we have supported firms in making reasonable accommodations, including the Employment Support for Employers to hire Persons with Disabilities scheme and ongoing work on a Tripartite Advisory.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also help them to build an adequate nest egg.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In the Budget speech, the Prime Minister announced the expansion of the Match Retirement Savings Scheme to include Singaporeans with disabilities, regardless of age, so long as they meet certain criteria.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And we will also continue to support the employment of ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Minister of State Gan Siow Huang will share more.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have improved our Workplace Safety and Health outcomes to be on par with developed countries, but we have to continue to stay vigilant.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Senior Minister of State Zaqy will share more.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We thank Mr Patrick Tay, Mr Louis Ng for their suggestions on the Employment Act, which we will consider in our review and I think we will share more later this year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And to guide employers to strengthen their capabilities, we have built up an ecosystem of support through the Institute for Human Resource Professionals and SNEF.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Mark Lee suggested enhancing CCPs for employees redeployed after M&As.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As I said in my Ministry of Trade and Industry COS speech, CCPs already offer substantial support for such workers, especially for mature workers, who may need more help during business transitions like mergers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We also thank Ms See on her points on the fair use of AI.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) has yet to encounter complaints of discrimination involving AI.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Chairman, I will say a few words in Mandarin.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: (In Mandarin):   As Confucius said, "At 30, I stood on my feet.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And at 50, I knew what destiny is in store for me." Similarly, MOM will help Singaporeans achieve their career aspirations at every stage of life.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For those new to the workforce or looking to switch careers, we will help unlock your career potential.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, we have enhanced the CCPs to help more workers, including those in flexi-load jobs, upgrade their skills.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If you are a working professional aiming to take your career to new heights, we will help you gain overseas work experience and expand your professional networks.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To our senior workers, please be assured: we will support your continued employment and help meet your basic retirement needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are also helping Singaporeans accumulate retirement savings through the Majulah Package, Silver Support Scheme and Matched Retirement Savings Scheme, for greater assurance in their golden years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We enhanced Workfare Skills Support to support your upskilling.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will build a safe, inclusive workplaces and ensure fair competition between local and foreign workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For businesses, we will support your transformation and talent development efforts to help you continue to thrive.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is a commitment by MOM to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government will work with employees and employers to build a better tomorrow. : In conclusion, Mr Chairman, today, the global order underpinning peace and prosperity has been upended in a matter of weeks.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But Singaporeans have the mettle and drive to navigate this turbulence and find new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We may be small, but we are nimble.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have never been defined by our limits, but by how we have responded to them and how we continue to respond to them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Through COVID-19, we have seen the adaptability and resilience of our businesses and workers even as we weathered crisis after crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In today’s world, the idea of a single job or rice bowl may no longer hold true, because change is not just constant, it is accelerating, and new challenges and disruptions will always emerge.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But we can forge something stronger, and that is the resilience, adaptability and courage to take on whatever comes next.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When one door closes, we will carve out a new path.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If the ingredients change, we can master new recipes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will walk with every Singaporean to help you journey through that change.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will help you realise your fullest potential, so long as you are willing to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: While we may not be certain of what lies ahead of us, one thing is certain.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government, workers and businesses together, coming in unity, in unison – we will achieve a brighter future for Singapore and for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The two tripartite workgroups will convene again this year to determine wage ladders for the next phase.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Employers support uplifting the livelihoods of our lower-wage workers, but many are grappling with business pressures.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Challenges such as a looming trade war, global economic uncertainty, rising cost of raw materials, e-commerce competition and the development of the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone are making our retail and F&B businesses rethink their strategies.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the concerns raised by businesses, what can the Ministry do to further strengthen the PWCS to support firms in raising wages beyond 2026.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Could the Ministry look into recognising enterprises who have attained the PW Mark with additional wage support?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Business owners have also shared the need to further streamline the PWM reporting process to the MOM and CPF.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Since the PWM has been in place since 2012, how can the Ministry refine reporting processes to reduce administrative burdens on businesses while maintaining accountability?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Many lower-income workers also have children relatively earlier in their lives.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This will provide a boost to those who are eager to take charge of their careers, lowering the financial hurdles they may face.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Career growth and skills developments should not be bound by age.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We want all Singaporeans, no matter where they are in their careers, to be equipped to succeed.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The sooner they get on board the train, the better.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, some low-wage workers aged below 30 have also been out of school and in the job market for a while and would benefit from more training opportunities.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How will the Government educate and encourage lower-wage workers over 30 to take up the longer courses that lead to deeper upskilling and better employment?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Will the Government consider expanding the Workfare Skills Support enhancements further, say to those over 25?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Chairman, it has been almost two years since the implementation of recommendations by the Tripartite Workgroup on Lower-Wage Workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What has been the progress of these efforts and what are the benchmarks that the MOM uses to measure success?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is heartening that the Government has taken the lead in making the Progressive Wage Mark a contractual obligation for Government tenders.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How many lower-wage workers have been uplifted through the PW Mark, beyond the companies that are subject to mandatory licensing and foreign worker requirements?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What more can we do to encourage companies to adopt the PW Mark?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Implementing PWM will help reduce attrition and hopefully, transform the industry into one that can provide a viable career for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Chairman, when our annualised fatal injury rate held steady at 1.0 per 100,000 workers for 2023 and the first half of 2024, I then cautioned that we must continue to work hard to keep our workplace accidents as low as we can.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Unfortunately, complacency seems to have set in for the construction sector.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Worryingly, it was reported that many of these incidents were due to the lack of basic safety measures or non-compliance with established safety measures.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The spike in workplace fatalities is deeply concerning, because every life lost is one too many.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Can MOM provide an update on the Safety Accountability, Focus and Empowerment (SAFE) measures implemented thus far?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How have these measures improved workplace safety and health ownership?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How are these SAFE measures expected to improve safety in the construction sector?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What is the Ministry's plan to sustain the collective tripartite efforts on total workplace safety and health (WSH), including efforts on occupational disease prevention?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Ensuring workplace safety and health is a never-ending endeavour.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What is the Ministry's plan to foster a stronger workplace safety culture at every company, beyond just enforcement?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Freelancers are part of the value chain to create and deliver a finished product.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Oftentimes, the imbalance of bargaining power between freelancers and service buyers means that freelancers are held in check by market reality when pricing their fees.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Thus, freelancers would tend to price their fees based on what the market is prepared to pay, without factoring in the cost of safeguarding their health and safety at work.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: In the context of the creative industry, service buyers such as creative production houses are vendors and contractors that are held in check by the market reality of tight timelines and tighter budgets imposed by commissioning firms and Government agencies.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Because of budget limitations, creative production houses could be apathetic towards putting in measures that safeguard the health and safety of freelancers, including guidance on a cap on the total hours of work on set and ensuring risk mitigation for higher-risk activities such as specialised rigging, smoke effects, stunts and the use of weapons.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean
text: Would the Ministry consider outlining safe work safeguards, such as reasonable hours of work for the creative and media industry?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: SMEs face even greater challenges, often lacking the resources to support employees' mental well-being.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: While larger firms can afford to provide mental health support and initiatives, SMEs struggle without dedicated infrastructure, leaving workers very vulnerable.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: I am grateful that the Government has introduced initiatives like the Total Workplace Safety and Health programme, offering free consultations, as well as HPB's integrated workplace mental health solution, which equips workplaces with wellness tools.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Yet with burnout widespread, especially in SMEs, more targeted support is needed.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Singapore will be super-ageing society as defined by the United Nations (UN) in 2026.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: As an ageing society, workplaces must be more inclusive and accommodative to the physical needs of a more senior staff base, from providing more ergonomic support to more aware of long-term work-related disorders.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: In addition, more attention and conversations can be situated around lifecycle changes such as menopause, which Duke-NUS has dubbed the Menopause Wave to come in a super-ageing Singapore.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Some progressive companies have put together menopause policies, which cover the physical and mental well-being of peri-menopause and menopause employees, but efforts are at best spotty.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Mental wellness is also an increasingly important workplace safety and health performance indicator, with around one in seven people in Singapore experiencing a mental disorder in their lifetime.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Studies have also suggested that work stressors were among factors associated with poor mental health.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Some workplaces have mental wellness champions, but more can be done to enhance the training and expertise of such champions.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: However, in practice, there could have been instances in which employers terminated employees in ways that were calculated to fly under the radar of retrenchment.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Employees might have been made to resign or are let go in the name of poor performance, even if employers were really planning to make their roles redundant and not planning to fill the vacancy any time soon.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, the affected employees feel like they are in fact being retrenched.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: If they file a case with the TADM, they can probably get a judgement in their favour, but affected employees might not have chosen to do so for various reasons and effectively they chose to forgo the retrenchment benefits that they ought to have received.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We know mature workers in their forties and fifties are especially affected by retrenchments in general.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: My guess is that they are also disproportionately affected by stealth retrenchments, as I just described.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Emotionally, for sure, but also financially, especially if the mature worker is sandwiched between children and elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And retrenchment done in stealth adds salt to the wound and cuts even deeper as the worker feels a sense of injustice, betrayal and suffering in silence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Chairman, I have long championed extending the productive longevity of our senior workers – not just to tackle demographic shifts, but because their experience, resilience and skills are invaluable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Yet, in our ageing society, are we truly harnessing this potential?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: The old-age support ratio has plunged from six in 2014 to 3.5 in 2024.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Are we underutilising a workforce that still has much to give?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: The employment rate for seniors aged 65 to 69 hit 47.5% in 2022.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: More seniors want to work, but are we offering them the right opportunities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: To our senior workers: lifelong learning is not just a buzzword.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: How can we better match skills to new roles, including those in the gig economy?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: I have pushed for tailored courses that align with seniors' interests and experience.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Are we doing enough to ensure that fair wages reflect their productivity?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: To employers: age-friendly workplaces are not just nice to have; they are a necessity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: But are they redesigning roles to make work more flexible?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Are job-sharing and hybrid arrangements becoming the norm, or the exception?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Could we proactively partner with businesses to create more opportunities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: It is time to rethink ageing in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Can we build a society where every individual, regardless of age, has a place to contribute meaningfully?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Mr Chairman, with increased life expectancy and Singaporeans being healthier, it is even more important to plan for retirement and retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Senior workers may also want to continue working with shorter hours, lighter workloads or flexible schedules.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: However, the employment of seniors will require a shift in mindset from all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Have our policies on senior employment, such as Senior Employment Credit, job redesign and flexible work arrangements made an impact on senior employment?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Are we starting to see seniors getting employed in better redesign jobs that leverage on their strength and experience?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Has job redesign provided more and enough opportunities for our senior workers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: While ensuring that our workforce is prepared for a longer retirement adequacy, workers must also plan for their extended career longevity by taking responsibility for their career and skills upgrading, especially as part of their career health check and retirement planning.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How can we help our workers plan for upskilling to enhance their employability and extend their career longevity?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Chairman, workforce transformation presents a valuable opportunity for businesses to address manpower challenges while tapping into a diverse and skilled labour pool.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: These measures would not only expand Singapore' workforce capacity but also provide businesses with more adaptable and sustainable manpower solutions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Chairman, while Singapore maintains a low unemployment rate and offers many career opportunities, securing meaningful employment remains a significant challenge for seniors, differently-abled individuals, and those with caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Have we moved the needle in expanding job opportunities for these groups of individuals?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Take, for example, SG Enables efforts to connect persons with disabilities to jobs while commendable, the employment rate for this group still remains relatively low.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Similarly, the Senior Employment Credit incentivises business to hire older workers, but if you were to ask any seniors looking for jobs, they will still share that age bias persist in hiring practices.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: FWAs, whether flexi-load, flexi-time or flexi-place have been promoted.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How do we go beyond schemes and incentives to truly shift workplace culture towards inclusive hiring practices?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: What more can be done to ensure that employment inclusivity is not just a policy goal, but a reality for all Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many in the LGBTQ+ community are relieved that Minister confirmed that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is covered under the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices (TGFEP).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This position is now reflected in Hansard on the Parliament website but strangely, not on the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) website.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, many of us in this House have been fighting hard for parent care leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have been asking serious questions of why legislate childcare leave but not parent care leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Are we signalling that looking after our children is more important than looking after our parents?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why provide parent care leave to all civil servants but not others?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It cannot only be that civil servants need to look after their parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government has said repeatedly that we are an ageing population.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The younger generation not only has to bear the tax burden but they will also need time to look after their parents, especially when they are ill.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As companies enforce return-to-office measures, many caregivers, especially single adults supporting elderly parents and parents of children with severe disabilities, face growing uncertainty.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For them, flexible work is not a convenience but a necessity for balancing caregiving and financial stability.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Single caregivers form the backbone of informal caregiving, often juggling full-time jobs at the cost of career progression and retirement security.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Some are even forced to leave the workforce entirely.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Since my 2022 speech on supporting single caregivers, we have seen progress.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: HDB now prioritises singles buying flats near elderly parents, and businesses must process flexible work requests, for which we are very grateful.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Yet, these policies fall short of guaranteeing approvals, leaving caregivers in limbo.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Likewise, for parents of children with severe disabilities, flexible work is essential, not a preference.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: How will the Government ensure that caregivers, especially singles supporting elderly parents and parents of children with disabilities, can remain in the workforce while meeting their caregiving responsibilities despite return-to-office mandates?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Caregivers have shared that flexible work arrangements (FWAs) are their most preferred form of support in balancing work and caregiving.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These guidelines are designed to address the fact that every caregiver’s needs are unique, and that these needs may evolve depending on job requirements and business realities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: FWAs implemented must be sustainable and create win-win outcomes for both employers and employees alike.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Progressive practices, which include setting up clear outcome-based KPIs for employees, implementing more frequent and regular check-ins with staff, and upskilling or equipping human resources personnel with current FWA practices must also be encouraged.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: More resources must also be availed to lesser resourced small and medium enterprises (SMEs) on implementing programmes and policies for the long-term sustainability of FWAs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some progressive employers have started to work with the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) on the creation of employee attraction and retention programmes using FWAs, such as the NTUC C U Back at Work Programme (CUB).

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Chairman: Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Chairman, I will now speak about the Ministry of Manpower's (MOM's) efforts to empower workers to build career health at all stages of their lives.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I will touch on four groups: first, for the broad base of workers, we will help you build up your career health and resilience; second, for those who lose their jobs involuntarily, we will support you to bounce back into employment; third, for our senior workers, we will do more to uplift your productive longevity; fourth, for our migrant workers, we will continue to support and improve their well-being.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In the past year, we have enjoyed higher-than-expected economic growth and favourable labour market outcomes.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We must continue to embrace innovation so that workers can progress into better jobs and businesses can generate growth that uplifts all Singaporeans.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We must also develop a future-ready workforce that can navigate changes in the job landscape and compete for good jobs.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Forward SG identified career agility and resilience as a key focus in our refreshed social compact.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In this age of change and disruption, we need better awareness of our career prospects, keep our skills relevant, stay on top of the competition and seize new opportunities.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To empower our workers to do so, we have launched Career Health SG, a nationwide initiative to help workers take charge of their careers and achieve their career aspirations.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: How do we take charge of our career health?

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Well, just as we look after our physical health by eating healthily, exercising regularly and having periodic medical check-ups, we encourage all Singaporeans to take charge of their own career health through three simple steps.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Just as we go for regular health screenings, we should regularly assess our career prospects and skillsets.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Instead of waiting till something goes wrong, we should take proactive steps to identify our skills gaps and career opportunities.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Just as we develop exercise and diet routines, we should chart our career and training goals.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We need to constantly review and update these career plans based on changes in the labour market and our stage of life.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We need to act on our plans to seek better jobs, upgrade our skills and stay competitive in the job market.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: By taking these three steps to take charge of one’s career health, we can ace our careers with better jobs, better wages and greater resilience.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To empower workers in this three-step journey, we are supporting our workers with jobs and skills insights to help them make informed training and career decisions.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The CareersFinder feature on the MyCareersFuture portal is one example of this.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: CareersFinder harnesses Government data and artificial intelligence (AI) to provide workers with personalised guidance and recommendations for suitable jobs based on their skills and expertise, and training opportunities based on their career goals.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We have seen encouraging signs of users broadening their job search horizons.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Gerald Giam highlighted the need to go beyond digital tools to support jobseekers with personalised and effective career coaching.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For those who prefer in-person guidance, we have taken steps to make quality career guidance more accessible.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We have piloted Polaris, where employed individuals can receive personalised career guidance from professionally certified career coaches.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Since November 2023, Polaris has benefited more than 620 individuals.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Over 90% reported gaining clearer direction and higher confidence in planning their own careers.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: One such participant is Ms Joanne Wang, the Regional Head of Marketing at Timezone.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: At 39, Joanne signed up for Polaris to better plan for her career and improve her management skills.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With advice from her WSG career coach, she decided to pick up professional coaching to further develop herself and her team.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In doing so, she boosted her team performance and her own career satisfaction.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Jobseekers can also receive support from WSG’s Volunteer Career Advisors, who draw from their own industry expertise to provide peer-level support and career advisory.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Under this initiative, individuals can receive sector- and occupation-specific insights to help them plan for their career or transition into new roles.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We also want to make quality career guidance even more accessible to all workers.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Some may hesitate to go for career guidance because they are concerned about the cost and are uncertain about the quality of service providers.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For a start, these credits can be used to offset Polaris' fees.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The list of endorsed providers will be expanded progressively, to help workers access quality career guidance.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Beyond career guidance, Mr Gerald Giam also emphasised the importance of quality career matching services.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This will enable jobseekers to find work near their homes to help them to balance work with personal commitments.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This will contribute to the diverse range of services in the employment facilitation landscape.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These services support all jobseekers, including those returning after a career break.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The services include: (a) career matching services offered by WSG’s Careers Connect, NTUC's Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) Career Centres, and Jobs and Skills Centres; as well as (b) services provided by WSG's appointed career-matching providers, like Ingeus and AKG.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: WSG also works with employers to reskill and place individuals into good growth jobs under programmes, like the Career Conversion Programmes (CCPs) and Mid-Career Pathways Programme.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Through these efforts, we hope to empower our workers to achieve their career goals.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Workers must also play their part to proactively upkeep their skills, regularly review their career plans and seize good job opportunities at every stage of their careers.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Investing in career health is a win-win for employers and workers.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Employers who do so can better attract and retain talent, sharpen their competitive edge and grow their businesses.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum asked how we can support employers to promote lifelong learning and skills development for their employees.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Government has continued to strengthen support for employers to invest in the career health of their workers, such as through WSG's CCPs.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These programmes have resulted in tangible career outcomes for employees.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Participants also improved their employment retention compared to non-participants.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This shows that our efforts to reskill workers have an extended, positive impact on their wages and career longevity.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Beyond supporting employers, we are also working hand-in-hand with employers to co-develop effective solutions.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: A key recommendation was to build employers' capabilities to guide employees in developing their skills and careers.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This entailed providing resources for employers to engage their employees in meaningful career development conversations.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In line with this recommendation, WSG has been piloting workshops for human resource (HR) professionals and line managers, to equip them to implement better-structured career conversations in their own organisations.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The AfA also found that employers who implemented an internal marketplace to support talent visibility and internal mobility better retained talent.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: One of the AfA member firms, Salesforce, introduced a Talent Community Platform with personalised career recommendations, training and resources for employees to navigate career paths within the company.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As a result, Salesforce enjoyed higher talent retention amidst fierce competition, with their employees better able to plan for their careers and upkeep their skills.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: MOM is working closely with tripartite and industry partners on resources to enable more employers, especially our SMEs, to implement their own internal marketplaces.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For employers to implement these recommendations successfully, they will need to strengthen their HR to move beyond support functions to play a more strategic role in championing workforce transformation.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This means taking proactive steps to identify critical and emerging skills, and charting plans to fill those gaps in their companies through hiring and workforce development.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Employers can tap on resources by the Institute for Human Resource Professionals, such as their job redesign playbook, to meet these increased demands on HR.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will continue to support employers to strengthen HR capabilities under the Tripartite Workgroup on Human Capital Capability Development that the Minister just announced.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will need the strong support of employers to uplift the career health of our workers and will continue to explore new ways to enable employers to do this while meeting their business needs.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For example, MOM and SkillsFuture Singapore rolled out the Careers and Skills Passport, and are working with partners, like JobStreet, to use Government-verified jobs and skills data to facilitate job application and hiring.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We encourage HR practitioners to tap on these initiatives to better understand their employees' skills profile.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This will support training, development and deployment, and better support your business growth.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Few countries have invested in such a holistic and integrated set of efforts to support career planning and workforce development.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This underscores our continued commitment to empower Singaporeans to thrive amid economic uncertainty.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Even as our workers build their career health and make progress along their career plans, life, unfortunately, can present curveballs.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Together with other SkillsFuture programmes, the JS scheme helps individuals better navigate their job search to regain employment, instead of rushing into ill-fitting jobs due to immediate financial pressures.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: During my time as Deputy Secretary-General in the Labour Movement, I encountered brothers and sisters who faced retrenchment.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Being retrenched can have a profound emotional impact, often triggering a mix of shock, fear, anger and even shame.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Many shared with me that they experienced a deep sense of loss, not just of job or income but also of identity and purpose.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Some may feel a loss of self-worth, especially if their job was tied closely to their sense of identity.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: During our Forward Singapore conversations, participants shared that instead of just giving handouts, a well-structured job seeking process that provides professional career facilitation support can help them regain their confidence as they navigate the job market.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The JS Scheme is therefore more than just financial payouts and a job.

speaker: ﻿The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Patrick Tay asked for more details on what the activities-based system will entail.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Members may also access these materials through the MP@SGPARL App.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As Members can see, jobseekers will be guided to complete meaningful activities like attending a career fair, updating their resume and going for career coaching.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We have carefully curated these activities based on user research with jobseekers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Jobseekers have shared with us that the framework is useful in helping them to regain employment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This activities-based system is also designed to ensure that jobseekers do not have to go through this journey alone.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They can tap on WSG's resources and speak to WSG's career coaches, allowing them to benefit from professional guidance.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Through these touchpoints, jobseekers will be more assured that they are on the right track to re-entering employment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As jobseekers embark on these activities as part of their job search journey, we hope to build up their confidence.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And when jobseekers eventually return to work, we hope they will regain their sense of identity and self-worth.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Take Mr Lim, who is retrenched from his job due to company restructuring.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Taskforce for Responsible Retrenchment and Employment Facilitation makes concerted efforts to reach out to all affected retrenched workers, such as Mr Lim, to offer career matching services.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Through this, Mr Lim books an appointment with a WSG career coach who provides him with advice on job applications based on his skills.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: He also applies and joins the JS scheme following the advice from his career coach.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: During this period, Mr Lim makes use of the comprehensive employment facilitation support offered under the scheme, such as career coaching, SkillsFuture courses and career fairs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: He also updates his resume and applies for jobs that match his skills, including those in less familiar roles or sectors.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: By making good use of the comprehensive support under the activities-based system, Mr Lim receives the guidance and financial support needed to build up his career health and bounce back into a well-fitting job.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Equipped with new skills and having found a new job, Mr Lim regains his sense of purpose and self-worth.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But I want to emphasise that the JS scheme should not be viewed in isolation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Government, in fact, has in place various other schemes to provide financial support for those undergoing substantial reskilling or experiencing financial hardships.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For example, if Mr Lim enrols in long-form training while job searching, he can apply for both the JS scheme and the SkillsFuture Level-up Programme.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Jobseekers from households with financial difficulties may also receive additional social assistance from ComCare based on their needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Involuntarily unemployed individuals can also visit WSG and NTUC e2i's centres island-wide for support in their job search.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The JS scheme will be an added boost to Singapore's ecosystem of support for unemployed individuals, empowering them to take ownership in navigating a difficult chapter of their lives, to emerge with better outcomes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The key is providing jobseekers with financial assistance, complemented by a robust ecosystem of training and employment facilitation support.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This way, we can strengthen our workers' career health and their longer-term prospects, and help them to rebuild their confidence to pursue better jobs and make bolder career moves.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is part of our desired social compact, where the Government will support you through difficult times, while you take personal responsibility and make an effort to overcome career setbacks and bounce back stronger.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Our population is ageing, and seniors today are living longer and healthier lives.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We want to enable seniors to continue working if they wish to, so that they can contribute their expertise and accumulate more savings for retirement.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This will also help employers meet manpower needs in a tight labour market.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Our policies over the past decade have paved the way for seniors to work longer.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This keeps us on track to meet our eventual goal of raising them to 65 and 70 respectively by 2030.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I am heartened that our Government and tripartite partners are taking the lead to implement the increases ahead of the national schedule.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Public Service and NTUC will be raising their retirement and re-employment ages to 64 and 69 this year, and SNEF has implemented the eventual goal of 65 and 70 since 2021.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I encourage all employers to start preparing for next year's increases.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As seniors work, we will also help them save more for retirement.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Since 2022, we have been implementing the Tripartite Workgroup on Older Workers' recommendation to increase Central Provident Fund (CPF) contribution rates for senior workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: At the same time, the Government will extend the CPF Transition Offset for another year.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This will help ease the transition for employers by covering half of the increase in employer contributions for 2026.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will continue to enhance our current measures to enable our seniors to work longer.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We hope this assures employers that the Government will support you to prepare for our ageing workforce.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Our efforts to help seniors extend their career runways have paid off.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Our labour force participation rate for those aged 60 to 69 was 59.7% in 2024, up from 55.8% in 2019.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We are proud to rank alongside the top five Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But there is more that can be done.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Today, seniors are leaving the labour force before 65, with many leaving in their 50s.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Our labour force participation rate falls from 86% for those aged 50 to 54, to 67.9% for those aged 60 to 64, a stark decrease of about 18 percentage points.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Some wish to slow down and focus on family or personal commitments.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Others have not worked for some time and may need to refresh their skills to return to the workforce.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Sharael Taha have highlighted that all stakeholders must play their part to effect broader societal shifts to support senior employment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Workers will need to embrace career changes over longer working lives.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Employers will need to redesign jobs and build capabilities for a multi-generational workforce.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Government will enable these shifts by working with our tripartite partners to develop targeted measures to drive senior employment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is the impetus behind the Tripartite Workgroup on Senior Employment, which I will be chairing alongside NTUC Deputy Secretary-General and Senior Minister of State Desmond Tan and SNEF's Vice President Ms Tan Hwee Bin.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As announced by the Prime Minister at Budget, this will be a significant tripartite effort to review and refresh our approach towards senior employment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It signals our tripartite commitment to co-creating solutions that meet the needs of workers and employers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Workgroup will focus on two key objectives.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: First, to empower senior workers to be productive and employable.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: With longer working lives, workers will need to continually upkeep their skills and remain open to trying new things in their late-stage careers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Desmond Choo and Mr Xie Yao Quan asked about what more we can do to train and place our senior workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Through the Workgroup, we will study better tailoring such services to suit seniors' preferences and needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For a start, WSG and its partners will provide targeted career guidance workshops for seniors to help them better plan for their later-stage careers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Second, to promote age-friendly jobs and multi-generational workplaces.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We want to support multi-stage careers, where workers can adjust their workload based on their needs and aspirations.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For example, Mr Desmond Choo and Mr Mark Lee suggested to scale up job redesign and fractionalised work that caters to senior workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will explore these ideas and much more under the Workgroup.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To kickstart this journey, the Workgroup will convene an Alliance for Action (AfA) on Empowering Multi-Stage Careers for Mature Workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This AfA will bring together diverse stakeholders to co-create new ideas and pilot innovative ways to make workplaces more age-friendly.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This echoes Mr Sharael Taha's point on going beyond schemes to shift workplace culture.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Instead of adopting a top-down approach, we want to take each step in collaboration with our stakeholders, so that positive change can truly take root and bear fruit.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: First, we will engage citizens from all walks of life to develop insights on the challenges and opportunities of an ageing workforce.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will hear from current and future seniors, as well as management and HR professionals representing employers of different sizes and sectors.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: By engaging widely, we can hear directly from stakeholders and build an enduring social compact together.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Second, we will work closely with employers to prototype innovative solutions to better support senior employment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Participating employers will receive funding and consultancy support to develop new models customised to their business needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will be opening applications to join the AfA soon, and I encourage all interested employers to sign up and be pathfinders for your industries.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In turn, the insights from the AfA will inform our approach towards senior employment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Chairman, allow me to say a few words in Mandarin.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: (In Mandarin):   Since 2022, we have been gradually increasing CPF contribution rates for senior workers to help them save more for retirement.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In 2026, the CPF contribution rates for those aged above 55 to 65 will increase by 1.5%.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: (In English): Sir, another group we want to support is our migrant workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We have made significant moves to improve their well-being in recent years.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Louis Ng suggested increasing penalties for employment kickbacks.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Ministry will not hesitate to press for the maximum penalties if a case warrants it.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This ensures that offenders cannot retain the illegal kickbacks.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will continue to work closely with our stakeholders to stamp out kickbacks and ensure that our migrant workers are treated fairly.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Chairman, in conclusion, the Government will be implementing several measures to empower Singaporeans of all walks of life to build their career health and seize good job opportunities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will uplift different segments of our workforce so that no one is left behind.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will continue to work closely with our tripartite partners and other stakeholders to develop a competitive workforce and support employers in their business growth.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Together, we can sustain our economic growth and build a shared future for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Members may also access these materials through the MP@SGPARL app.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Chairman, for many years, tripartism has been the critical success factor to raising the incomes and skills of our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This helps narrow the gap with the median and, at the same time, keeps this sustainable for businesses.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This results in meaningful wage increases for our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Increases are set at a pace that is sustainable for employers and mapped out over a period, which gives predictability for contracting and business planning.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: What does this mean for Singapore's workers and businesses and why does PWM work?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: PWM works because we do not just rely on a minimum wage line to boost wages – but we rely on PWMs that boost wages for workers across different sectors and occupations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Negotiated PWMs are impactful because we can optimise wage increments in different sectors, taking into consideration workforce productivity, sectoral growth and business transformation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: From a holistic perspective, this means that we can maximise the wage growth potential of different sectors, such as security, waste management and others, and help our workers and their wages to grow.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is also about mapping out skills and career pathways.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This supports productivity improvements and provides workers with progression prospects.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Collectively, PWM sets the pace for wage growth, with Local Qualifying Salary (LQS) shoring up as our last line.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have a progressive and sustainable system, one that works, unlike a traditional minimum wage system.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: PWMs form a network of ladders in the ecosystem, leading the way to improve the wage outcomes for our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Tripartism is, therefore, our "secret sauce" in providing that balance that, in doing so, we keep businesses sustainable, so that they can continue to hire workers and can sustain their wage growth over time.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We cannot take this balance for granted, nor should allow politics to take over and start auctioning minimum wage levels.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have seen how this has played out in many countries – a blunt minimum wage line determined by politics, or rather, auctioned by politics just to win elections.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Some are unsustainable and fail to be implemented; others are pushed through but the industry cannot keep pace.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, businesses just hire fewer workers or reduce their work hours.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, businesses lose out and workers lose out.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Our tripartite partners are keenly aware of these drawbacks and therefore, for PWM, we negotiate outcomes in the best interests of our people's livelihoods and a sustainable economy.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In fact, why offer our Singapore lower-wage workers the minimum when they can already benefit from progressive wages today?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked about the impact of our efforts and I am proud to share that our tripartite efforts have yielded good, tangible outcomes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Lower-wage workers have consistently seen strong wage growth.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If Members will refer to the handout distributed, our Lower-wage Workers Chart, you will find a chart of all of our lower-wage workers' wage growth that is coming up, in the coming years, especially in the different sectors.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And for sectors like security, for example, we have seen very good and strong progress.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: When it started in 2016, the PWM requirement was $1,300.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: That, I think, shows how progressive PWM is today.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It means that even though costs of living rose, the wages of our lower-wage workers rose even more.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, the wage gap between lower-wage workers and the median worker is also narrowing, even while median wages continue to rise.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In fact, a big part of this growth took place in the last three years, when tripartite partners agreed to expand PWM to three additional sectors and to two additional occupations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In the Department of Statistics' (DOS') latest report, income inequality in Singapore, as measured by the Gini coefficient, has declined steadily over the last decade.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, this bucks the trend, compared to many other countries where income wage gaps are widening.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Here, we have seen the Gini coefficient reduced and I would like to think that PWM had played a role in this, too.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, I am hopeful that this will continue in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And this is a reflection of the tripartite partners' relentless efforts – our partners from the union, our partners from the employers, and as well as partners from the Government – for their unwavering commitment.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Besides tripartite partners to drive wage growth, the Government also provides lower-wage workers with additional support through the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) Scheme, what we typically know as Workfare, and we have enhanced this further.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And this ensures that WIS continues to help workers in the bottom 20th income percentiles, with some support for those slightly above.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The maximum payment has been raised to $4,900 per year, up from $4,200.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Those aged 60 and above will benefit from this highest payment tier, as well as persons with disabilities, regardless of age.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: WIS payments for all other age groups have also been increased.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These enhancements to WIS will benefit about half a million lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Government will continue to work with tripartite partners to help lower-wage workers strengthen their wage and employment outcomes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Melvin Yong would be happy to hear that the tripartite partners are currently studying the expansion of PWM to the Pest Management sector and will provide more details in due course.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Above all, as Mr Edward Chia, Mr Fahmi Aliman and Mr Neil Parekh highlighted, the key to raising wages sustainably over the long term is for both workers and businesses to become more productive.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Businesses must transform low-wage jobs for higher value-add and improve the efficiency of their operations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At the same time, with better jobs created, there will be demand for new skillsets and competencies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workers will need to upskill to seize these opportunities and we will step up our efforts to help them do so.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Since 2010, the Government has been supporting low-wage workers in their upskilling journey through the Workfare Skills Support scheme, or WSS.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Currently, WSS is targeted at short courses that can be completed over a few days.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It covers the opportunity costs of training for low-wage workers aged 30 and above.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For example, those pursuing training on their own receive a training allowance of $6 per hour.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: However, low-wage workers stand to benefit more from long-form courses that provide more robust upskilling and reskilling, which are associated with more significant wage increments.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The challenge, of course, is that these take longer and the opportunity cost for low-wage workers is, therefore, also higher.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is targeted at helping low-wage workers who wish to pursue long-form training.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Taking reference from the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme, WSS (Level-Up) will provide low-wage workers who pursue long-form training with substantially higher training allowance, to cover the higher opportunity costs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Part-time trainees will receive a fixed monthly allowance of $300.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is more than three times higher than the training allowance currently provided by WSS.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We also recognise that workers in lower-wage jobs may need more bouts of long-form training across their career stages.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is to acquire the necessary skills for more complex job roles, or pivot to new sectors.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Hence, WSS (Level-Up) will cover up to 24 months of long-form training done before the age of 40 and another 24 months of long-form training after the age of 40.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: WSS (Level-Up) will be rolled out from early 2026.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We will provide more details later this year.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar also asked if there are plans to extend WSS to low-wage workers aged 25 and over.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We will keep this suggestion in mind, but at the same time, there are no plans to do so, as there are other schemes that younger workers can tap on, such as the ITE Progression Award and SkillsFuture Credit.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For low-wage workers to put their newly acquired skills to good use, businesses must also transform low-wage jobs for higher value-add and refine their processes for higher productivity.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, upskilling is just one half of the equation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There has been encouraging progress on the business front.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In the retail and food services sector, businesses are adopting technological solutions, such as self-service systems and RFID inventory management.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, instead of routine tasks, retail workers can take on more diversified and higher-skilled jobs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In outsourced sectors, such as cleaning, security and waste management, service providers are adopting robots and Internet-of-Things (IoT) solutions to reduce reliance on labour-intensive operations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, existing workers can then be retrained and deployed to higher-value roles.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Government understands that it takes time for workers to upskill and for businesses to transform.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In the near term, businesses are also concerned about manpower costs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We recognise that uplifting our low-wage workers will lead to some increases in manpower costs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But in a typical business organisation, low-wage workers account for a relatively modest share of businesses' overall manpower costs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: They constitute only about one-fifth of our resident workforce and their wages are relatively lower to begin with.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Nonetheless, we hear employers' concerns over the broader cost pressures.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This builds on three earlier rounds of PWCS enhancements.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In fact, since 2022, the Government has co-funded the majority of wage increases given to low-wage workers and this was added up to 75% and 50% in previous years.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The upcoming PWCS enhancements will continue to provide short-term relief, but I strongly encourage employers to make use of this opportunity to accelerate your transformation, so that we can uplift low-wage workers sustainably over the long term.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Chairman, we have made good progress so far, but we must press on with our efforts to uplift low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We must all work together to reduce income inequality, which can cause risks in society if left unchecked.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Over the next two years, the tripartite partners will be negotiating the next bound of wage schedules for the PWMs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Government has laid the groundwork for this through PWCS, which supports business transformation efforts and brings some relief to cost pressures.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We hope that employers and consumers, too, will play their part in uplifting our low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Chairman, as we uplift the livelihood of our workers, we must also safeguard their lives.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Our performance for Workplace Safety and Health (WSH), has improved over the years.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: While the WSH performance of sectors, such as manufacturing has improved, others can and must do better.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We can certainly do much better for construction, which remains the top contributor of workplace accidents today.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked for an update on the Safety Accountability, Focus and Empowerment measures (SAFE).

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: All SAFE measures have been implemented over the last few years.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: They are a comprehensive set of measures aimed at enhancing collective WSH ownership.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At the sectoral level, we enhanced businesses' incentive to prioritise safety by disqualifying poor WSH performers from tendering for public sector construction projects.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This helps contractors to identify WSH hazards and facilitates MOM's investigations and deters unsafe behaviours.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At the company level, chief executives and board directors in higher-risk sectors, including construction, must attend the Top Executive WSH Programme to understand their duties and learn how to foster good safety practices in their companies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Beyond safety, we agree with Mr Melvin Yong that it is equally important to safeguard the health of our workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, moving forward, we will continue to work with industry partners, employers and unions to focus on areas of preventive health and occupational health, in support of national initiatives, such as Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Everyone must continue to do our part, to build a strong WSH culture.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Company directors must drive home the importance of safety within their organisations and good WSH is integral to business success.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workers are responsible for following safe work procedures to protect themselves and others.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Unions must advocate for safe, healthy workplaces and working conditions, for example, by developing WSH champions in each union.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The public can report unsafe workplace practices to MOM, as each report can save a life.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Ms Jean See asked about shared responsibility for workplace safety in the creative industry.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Service buyers must play their part by ensuring that their contractors, including freelancers, have the necessary competency to work safely.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Contractors must work safely and not engage in risk-taking behaviour.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The WSH Guidelines on Event Management provide practical guidance on health and safety requirements relevant to the creative industry.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Together, we can achieve our WSH 2028 goal of reducing and sustaining the fatality injury rate at below 1.0 per 100,000 workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Chairman, I started my speech with how tripartism in Singapore is Singapore's "secret sauce" that empowers our low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: That, in turn, uplifts their families and communities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: More than that, this harmonious partnership among our unions, businesses and the Government weaves the fabric of a resilient and prosperous Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Chairman, much has been said about our workforce and workplaces transforming.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: What remains unchanged is our commitment to ensure that every member of society is able to participate fully in the workforce and achieve their aspirations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Allow me to, first, share how we are enhancing support for persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
