text: Our objective is to raise awareness and shape mindsets around the concept of reasonable accommodations in the workplace, guiding employers and employees to discuss accommodations that will suit their specific work context and needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This will support persons with disabilities in employment, giving them the chance to thrive in the workplace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Government also encourages the hiring and training of persons with disabilities through SG Enable's Open Door Programme, which provides grants and employment support services to organisations that hire persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Under EEC, eligible employers of persons with disabilities receive a wage offset of up to $400 per month.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This goes up to $800 per month for the first nine months of employment if the new hire was previously not working for at least six months.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Sharael Taha and other Members would be glad to hear that since its introduction in 2021, the EEC has contributed to the steady increase in the employment rate of persons with disabilities, which rose from 28% to 34% over the past five years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: One individual who has benefited from the EEC is Emily.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Despite the challenges she faces due to her intellectual disability, Emily has been keen to work and persevered through her job search.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: After completing training at the Centre for Inclusive Employment at the Enabling Business Hub @ Jurong, her job coach matched her to a job in packing and order fulfilment with Zyfas Pharma Pte Ltd Singapore, a pharmaceutical products wholesaler.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: With support from her job coach and supervisor, Emily is doing well in her job and has been converted to permanent employment since January 2025.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Besides attaining greater financial independence, Emily's new role has enabled her to become more confident through greater participation in the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We also want to support persons with disabilities to save more for their retirement needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Today, under the Matched Retirement Savings Scheme (MRSS), the Government provides a dollar-for-dollar matching grant to encourage CPF top-ups for eligible Singaporean seniors from age 55.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This will help individuals like Emily to accumulate their savings for retirement earlier.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: They will be able to benefit from the compounding effect of CPF interest over a longer runway.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For example, a 25-year-old person with disability who receives a top-up of $2,000 every year up to the lifetime cap of $20,000 will receive about $110,000 more just in CPF interest alone by the age of 65, as compared to an individual who receives top-ups from 55 years old.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We hope such efforts will help persons with disabilities build up their nest eggs early and approach retirement with a greater sense of security.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For ex-offenders looking to rejoin the workforce, the idea of reintegration can feel daunting at times.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: However, they are not alone in this journey.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: WSG partners with Yellow Ribbon Singapore, which provides employment assistance and post-placement support to inmates and ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These initiatives are further supported by the Uplifting Employment Credit which provides wage offsets to employers that hire ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In 2024, the Uplifting Employment Credit supported the employment of more than 1,500 ex-offenders hired by about 700 employers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Under the Uplifting Employment Credit, eligible employers of ex-offenders can receive a wage offset of up to $600 per month for the first nine months of employment, amounting up to $5,400 for each new ex-offender hired.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: One such individual who has benefited is John, not his real name, who secured employment with a communication services company in 2023.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As an associate engineer, John provided backend support for customer accounts that were assigned to him.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Over time, his duties expanded to include tasks like data analytics work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Today, John’s company continues to support his professional development by employing him in upskilling courses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For John, the reintegration process has been challenging but rewarding.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Reflecting on his journey, he shared: "The hardest part of reintegration was believing in myself again.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I am grateful to the company for hiring me and trusting my ability to value add to the organisation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This job has been crucial in rebuilding that self-confidence".

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As John continues to grow in his new role, his success story is helping to reshape perceptions of ex-offenders, paving the way for more inclusive hiring practices in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Next, I will share more on our efforts to support the employment of women and caregivers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Many women shoulder the caregiving responsibilities for their children, elderly parents or family members with disabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some caregivers have had to take a break from their careers to care for their family members full-time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: While others are able to continue working, they deal with challenges like burnout as they try their best to balance the demands from work and family.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Whether at home or at work, we want women and caregivers to feel supported in managing their roles and be empowered to pursue their career aspirations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This means more women who wish to remain in work or return to work have found the opportunities to do so.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: However, as Mr Desmond Choo, Ms Yeo Wan Ling and Miss Rachel Ong have pointed out, there is room to do more, and we agree.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Mark Lee suggested better support for training of part-time workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We are enhancing the Career Conversion Programmes (CCPs) to support reskilling of mid-career new hires and employees on jobs with flexi-load arrangements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: CCPs provide employers with salary support when they reskill mid-career new hires or existing employees into growth job roles identified under the Industry Transformation Maps or Jobs Transformation Maps.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To qualify, they must be reskilled into growth job roles and be employed on permanent terms or contract terms of at least one year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For instance, a cybersecurity company looking to hire a part-time employee can now tap on the CCPs to hire and reskill a mid-career worker from another sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Besides making part-time work more viable, we are building on our efforts to foster family-friendly workplaces so that workers can give their best at work and at home.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Louis Ng has called for parent care leave to support caregivers of elderly parents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We are open to ideas on how to better support caregivers, including those who wish to work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: When considering additional leave, we must be mindful to balance caregivers’ needs with the potential impact on businesses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Working caregivers have also highlighted that flexible work arrangements (FWAs) are a more sustainable way to manage work and caregiving responsibilities, which is something that we have made progress on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As Mr Sharael Taha pointed out, building inclusive workplaces requires a shift in workplace culture and norms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Tripartite Guidelines on FWA Requests launched in April last year aim to facilitate this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Edward Chia would be glad to hear that we are working closely with trade associations and chambers, as well as our community partners, to raise awareness of the guidelines and help both employers and employees understand how the guidelines can help them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some partners have even gone further to develop resources to support their members in adhering to the Guidelines and implementing FWAs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For instance, the Singapore Business Federation (SBF) has helped raise awareness of the Guidelines through briefing sessions and these have reached more than 650 companies thus far.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling asked for an update on the outcomes of the Guidelines.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As these Guidelines have only been in effect for three months, it will take some to observe its impact on workplace norms and culture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: However, I am happy to see that the Guidelines have prompted more open conversations about FWA requests.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As an employer in the manpower-tight retail sector, Sheng Siong is leveraging FWAs as part of its strategy to retain employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The company recently introduced staggered working hours for their office employees, as well as options for alternative work schedules for those in frontline operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For example, instead of a standard six-day work week, frontline employees may request for a five-day, four-day or even three-day work week, with commensurate adjustments in the salary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Firms such as Sheng Siong are continuing to explore how they can leverage FWAs to better attract and retain talent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: On supporting women to take up leadership roles, Mr Desmond Choo suggested mandating that 40% of company boards comprise of women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: But such measures to mandate some kind of quota, if there are not enough women who are ready for such roles, could actually unintentionally affect the credibility of women at the workplace over the long term.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Singapore has put in place voluntary targets to accelerate the representation of women on boards and we have seen good progress.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To build inclusive workplaces we have taken steps to strengthen fair and merit-based employment practices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Louis Ng suggested clarifying on TAFEP’s website that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is covered under the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices (TGFEP).

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The TGFEP covers all forms of workplace discrimination and the listing on the website is not meant to be exhaustive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Highlighting selected characteristics or scenarios may not achieve this broader intent and may give the impression that characteristics or scenarios which are not mentioned are not covered.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: On supporting the well-being of workers in the workplace, I would like to thank all those who have raised suggestions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ms Hazel Poa suggested increasing the number of public holidays by three days for Hari Raya, Thaipusam and Chinese New Year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked for the inclusion of Thaipusam as a public holiday, echoing similar requests by other Members such as Mr Gan Thiam Poh in the past.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The current configuration of public holidays in Singapore is the outcome of careful deliberations and consultations with various religious groups at the point of Singapore’s Independence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Over the years, we have learnt to live harmoniously as a multi-ethnic and multi-religious society, with everyone making some compromises for the greater good.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We encourage employers to make it possible for Singaporeans of all faiths to observe their respective religious festivals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Maintaining the current balance has served us well, and it continues to be the sensible approach for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling, Mr Edward Chia and Miss Rachel Ong asked how we can continue to promote mental wellness in our workplaces, especially amongst SMEs that may not have built up dedicated infrastructure to support such initiatives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To equip companies, especially SMEs, with the resources and know-how, the tripartite partners have rolled out various initiatives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: A key initiative is the Tripartite Advisory on Mental Well-Being at Workplaces introduced in 2020.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: It provides practical guidance on measures that employers can adopt, such as tapping on Employee Assistance Programme to offering counselling support for employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Beyond the consultations and workshops offered by the Total Workplace Safety and Health Programme, SkillsFuture Singapore has also funded various courses relating to mental wellness for self, peers and employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Training Providers for such courses are able to contextualise the content to suit the needs of organisations, including SMEs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Further support is also available through the Well-being Champions Network and National Council of Social Service’s Peer Support Specialist Programme, which offer additional resources and training for workplace mental well-being.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Chairman, I will now say a few words in Mandarin.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This amount will be increased to $800 per month for the first nine months of employment if the newly hired employee with disabilities has not been employed in the previous six months.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Under the Uplifting Employment Credit scheme, employers who hire ex-offenders can receive up to $600 per month in credits during the first nine months of employment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This will help them start accumulating retirement savings earlier and benefit from CPF compound interest. : With your permission, Mr Chairman, may I ask the Clerk to distribute an infographic that summarises the support schemes available at different life stages?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Members may also access these materials through the MP@SGPARL application.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: As Minister Tan See Leng shared yesterday, the Government is committed to supporting every Singaporean in their career journey at every life stage, and with greater support for those in need.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: While the Government has a role to play in empowering our people, we also recognise that true transformation requires the support and action of those at the heart of our economy – our businesses, workers, tripartite partners and community partners.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For that, I thank all those who have worked closely with us.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Together, we can break down barriers, challenge stereotypes and continue to build an inclusive society where everyone has the opportunity to contribute meaningfully and play a role in our shared progress.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I will try to get as many across as possible.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The same usual request – keep your clarifications short and succinct.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: One, why is the Ministry raising the S Pass qualifying salary despite the labour market being already quite tight and the potential economic headwinds?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: What is the expected impact on the local workforce's wages?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Second, MOM is raising the maximum employment age for Work Permit holders and aligning it to the local retirement age.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Would the increase in the maximum employment age of Work Permit holders result in increased healthcare and insurance costs borne by the employers and also increase the competition for jobs with senior workers?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) chairman, Mr Desmond Choo, for raising the clarifications.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It does not lead market wages, but it is actually adjusted in line with what the prevailing wage is.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As I have shared extensively yesterday in my COS speech, we do this as we need to continue to raise productivity and not just have a case of just pure numbers coming in alone, but we do this to ensure our S Pass holders are of high quality.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the same time, we want to maintain a level playing field for our locals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have also said earlier on that we have announced this S Pass qualifying salary increase since COS 2022.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We said that it is over three steps.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This allows businesses the runway to plan ahead and to make the necessary adjustments.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To the second point about why we raised the maximum employment age, we took in feedback, significantly, again, from the different business chambers, the different trade associations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: What we have done is to give them the breadth, the latitude and also the runway for them to assess what is in their own best interests.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I note that for specific occupations such as cooks, companies can hire Work Permit holders from Laos, Cambodia and Bhutan, in addition to another seven odd countries.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: First, how will MOM step up efforts to foster inclusiveness and fair practices like reasonable work hours in the food sectors?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Second, how will MOM help workers from these new Non-Traditional Source countries to acclimatise to the work intensity in Singapore?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The third is to protect these new groups from being exploited by recruiters in their home countries.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Is MOM planning to facilitate direct outreach and referral programmes to bridge them to jobs in Singapore?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To Senior Minister of State Koh, I would like to ask about the JS scheme.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Could the scheme consider on a case-by-case basis self-employed persons such as creative freelancers who can prove income loss over a continual period because their jobs were cancelled or contracts were ceased when their work was offshored or due to AI substitution?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are also socialising these Non-Traditional Source countries with many of the SMEs and also the business owners themselves.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: By widening it, we hope that they can assess for themselves these options.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We work with different agencies, not just working in an insular fashion within MOM itself.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We work with, of course, security agencies, for instance.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We work with our economic agencies, of which I am Second Minister for Trade and Industry.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We obviously work with the Ministry of Trade and Industry to assess the fit.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Once they have buy-in from many of the business owners, the assessment is really up to the business owners to see whether they want to access the workforce from these Non-Traditional Source countries.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When they are onboarded, before they come into Singapore to work, they come in at our onboarding centres.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: What we hope to do is to also be able to socialise them to some of the expectations, the cultural norms, the living conditions and most importantly, what their rights are, the necessary helplines, the social agencies that are available to help them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have got different non-governmental organisations, including the Foreign Domestic Worker Association for Social Support and Training (FAST), which is a separate initiative from MOM's Assurance, Care and Engagement (ACE) division, to engage them, to assess the feedback.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If they run into problems, we will not hesitate to step in.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, broadly, the framework is there for them to access.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the same time, we are also very careful.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are very deliberate and very calibrated in terms of opening the Non-Traditional Source countries.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We do not open it up in a very extensive manner.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think the Senior Minister of State will cover the balance of your questions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Self-employed individuals do negotiate for projects on their own.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Sometimes, even if the project cannot take place, it could well be a mismatch between what the self-employed person's expectation of his own remuneration from the project owner is, or it could just be a business deal that could not take place because the negotiation did not succeed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But as long as the market wage exceeds this floor, which it could, for any given job in any given sector, although I acknowledge Minister Tan's point that it is pegged to the top third of overall salaries, then we could encounter a situation where a local could still be outcompeted by a foreigner so long as that Singaporean cannot accept a take home salary that is too low compared to a foreigner who is willing to accept a slightly lower gross income, but still receives a take home salary that is higher, just because —

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: On the call for the consideration of Thaipusam, I had cited in the conclusion of my cut former Minister EW Barker's implicit promise to revisit our public holiday schedule should our economy prosper.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Could I ask the Ministry if there are no economic conditions or no level of prosperity under which the Government will be willing to consider the schedule of public holidays?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: My personal view, and I am not an economist, but I think he looks at it from a fairly theoretical and academic viewpoint.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In reality, today we have a very tight labour market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I have repeatedly stated in this House that our businesses, our SMEs, our large local enterprises, these are owned and run by Singaporeans too.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They have constantly harped on the fact that there are significant manpower constraints, resource constraints for them to grow and expand their business.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, in this kind of very tight labour market, when you peg it at the qualifying salaries at the top one-third of the respective sector, we are not setting up a new forward projected qualifying salary.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The way we set the benchmarks is based on the prevailing salary of the top one-third of the EP and S Pass holders.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And our definition of unemployment is at that spot in time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Long-term unemployment is defined as someone who is unemployed for more than six months.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, if you take off the unemployment rate of about 2.8%, let us say, take away the long-term unemployment rate of 0.7% or 0.8%, that 2% delta is actually churned within six months – these people find a new job, or they find something that fulfils their calling and they get on to a new career, perhaps to a new calling.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I want to again emphasise today: does anyone think that we have an issue?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our issue is a very, very tight labour market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have Mr Mark Lee here, our Nominated Member of Parliament, who has repeatedly called for the Government to help businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: You could check with him after this debate to see how tight the situation is.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Chairman, as I said earlier, the decision on which public holidays to observe was only reached after very careful consultation with religious groups in Singapore in the past which, undoubtedly, required difficult decisions for the leaders from each faith to take.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Any move to reinstate a festival, such as Thaipusam, as a public holiday, may invite competing claims from members of other communities, both religious and non-religious.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Maintaining the current balance has served Singapore well and continues to be the sensible approach.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Regardless of the intervening years and the progress that we have made, this is a sensitive issue.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We should not take Singapore's economic progress for granted and look to introducing additional public holidays at every opportunity.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: And while we cannot designate all important festivals public holidays, there must be understanding and regard given for Singaporeans to observe occasions that are significant to them.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: That is why we urge all employers to show understanding and flexibility in this regard.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The first set is to Minister Tan See Leng.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Given that there could be other sources of labour which are in higher demand by businesses, could the Minister for Manpower explain how MOM decided on the list of countries for the Non-Traditional Sources occupation list?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The second set of clarifications is for Minister of State Gan Siow Huang.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) careers are high-value career choices and can move the needle in further closing the gender pay gap.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: What more can the Ministry do to encourage young women to consider careers in STEM as well as equipping female mid-careerists to convert into STEM careers?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Additionally, given the recent development to support caregivers to stay in the workplace, what steps will the Government take to ensure that the gender pay gap does not widen further for female caregivers who opt for alternative work arrangements, including FWAs, due to caregiving responsibilities?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On how we decide on the list of countries to be included, we, like many, many other countries in the world, carefully regulate the profile of non-citizens for our beloved country, Singapore, including those who wish to work here.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: One constraint is that we are a small and very densely populated city state.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And because of our constraints, we need to carefully, very delicately, balance infrastructure, security, social and economic considerations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We constantly work closely, calibrating with other Ministries, other sector agencies to assess the suitability of new sources, taking into account the earlier considerations that I have elaborated on.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Singapore's adjusted gender pay gap compares favourably with other countries, such as the United States and Canada, both of which are around 8%.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The key factor driving gender pay gap in Singapore is occupational segregation.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: In other words, there tends to be a lower share of females in higher paid occupations, such as business development managers, managing directors, chief executives and general managers.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We will continue to work with tripartite partners and community stakeholders to support women's participation in the workforce and help them enter and remain in occupations of their choice, including in traditionally male-dominated industries.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This way, women do not fall behind their male colleagues in terms of career, experience, progression and hence, wages.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This includes measures, such as FWAs, promoting shared-caregiving responsibilities at home, as well as career drives, networking and mentorship programmes.

speaker: The Chairman
text: There are still many, many hands from those who have filed four cuts.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I will give the floor to Mr Leong.

speaker: The Chairman
text: He only raised one cut, but it was a long cut.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First of all, I would like to thank the Minister for his energetic response to my arguments.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, because I think our views are still very different, I have —

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, first question, can I confirm that MOM still does not track the change in work pass holders that turned to PRs in the resident PME statistics?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If yes, does the Minister agree that there is no way to conclude definitively that the existing resident PMETs have not been displaced and become underemployed because all the statistics that he has quoted are affected by this effect?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Second question, the platform workers are a good example of the underemployed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Minister has admitted that about one-third of the platform workers, or 28,000, are involuntary.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But for many of the balance of the 70,000 platform workers who have preferred platform work for flexibility, does the Minister think that low wages and poor prospects are also a factor in their decisions?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Leong, if I could ask, how many clarifications?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Because I am conscious of the guillotine time.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Okay, make them short so that we can give enough time for the Minister to answer.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Third question, the increase in part-time workers and contract work are also examples of underemployment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can the Minister explain why we do not need to be concerned that the proportion of part-time workers out of all employed residents has increased from 8.4% in 2009 to 10.1% in 2023, and can the Minister quote the corresponding increase in resident contract workers in the same period, 2009 and 2023?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Last question, does the Minister agree that while wage growth may be faster than some developed countries like the United Kingdom, it is meaningless if the wage growth is still not enough to catch up with the escalating cost of living and housing prices in Singapore?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I will cover some parts of his point just to put it to rest, hopefully once and for all, before I hand over to my colleague, Minister for National Development, Mr Desmond Lee, who will also talk about housing, in just a while.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To the Member's clarification about part-time work and that he thinks that many of them are underemployed, I have actually shown in my explanation yesterday that the statistics that we have on time-related underemployment are very, very low and, in fact, it has dropped.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do not have the statistics offhand, but please refer to the Hansard on what I said yesterday.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, let me put that to rest once and for all.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Please do not forget that many, many of our naturalised Singaporeans, many of our Permanent Residents (PRs) are married to a local-born Singapore Citizen, and I really hope we should not keep harping on a "us versus them" mentality, because Singapore is a largely immigrant nation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are all here because we love this country.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: My father, and I am pretty sure Mr Leong's father, also were not local-born Singapore Citizens.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I benefited from here, just as he has, and we both want to do our best to serve our country.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I will invite Minister Desmond Lee to respond to the clarification on housing.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I assume this is in relation to what Mr Leong raised in his cut.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to apologise to Minister Tan See Leng and Members who had filed cuts at MOM's COS, for taking up some time.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Yesterday, Mr Leong made two points in his speech: first, he spoke about selective use of data on Singaporean and PR employment; and second, he said that Singaporeans today are worse off than in the past and he used the example of public housing, comparing the Housing and Development Board (HDB) affordability for university and Vocational and Industrial Training Board (VITB) graduates in 1979, with affordability today.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These were not raised at the Ministry of National Development's (MND's) COS at all.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Member did not speak at MND's COS, nor raise any clarification.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I checked and would like to make a few points to add to what Minister Tan said yesterday.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: He spoke about the situation, the improvements in our graduate situation, and I will talk about housing.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr Leong used the median wages of VITB graduates in 1979, but he did not mention that back then, only 9% of each cohort went to VITB.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, the vast majority of each cohort today go to university, polytechnic and ITE; compared to only around 13% going to university and VITB back in 1979.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr Leong was comparing housing affordability for a small group in 1979 with housing affordability for the vast majority of Singaporeans today.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: He also did not present the affordability picture for the majority of Singaporeans back in 1979, who were less well-educated, less skilled and earned much less in those early days of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Second, the HDB flat in 1979 is also very different from the HDB flat in 2025.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In the 1970s, HDB flats were simple, functional homes in estates with few amenities and very limited transport links.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Today, our flats come with modern amenities, far better transport connectivity, offering residents a higher standard of living.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In 1979, only 68% of our population lived in HDB, of whom 62% owned their flats.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is not surprising because the university and VITB graduates that Mr Leong cited yesterday were at the higher end of the income spectrum.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Today, more than 80% of Singaporeans live in HDB homes and over 90% own their flats.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Third, the housing market in 1979 was very different too.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In the 1960s and 1970s, there was almost no resale market to speak of.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In the 1960s, buyers had to return the flat to HDB at the sum that was less than what they had initially paid for.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In the 1970s, there was a very rudimentary resale market with strict conditions and limited financing.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Back then, there was limited potential for appreciation, it was not quite the store of value, it was a basic home and expense for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The resale market only started to mature in the 1980s and 1990s, after changes in conditions for resale and mortgage financing policies.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Today, our HDB flats are both a home and also a store of value for Singaporeans, which they can monetise in their older years for retirement by selling on the open market, renting out a room or a flat, through our Lease Buyback Scheme and so on.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We also wondered why Mr Leong was so selective in using the year 1979; and we realised why.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: From 1968 to 1987, in the early years of HDB, we sold flats to Singaporeans and the flat price was fixed to recover cost.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, this most resembles the Progress Singapore Party's (PSP's) Affordable Housing Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, in a way, PSP's idea is not an original idea, but an idea adapted from the past.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: HDB flats back in those days were priced based on construction costs.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The PSP's Affordable Housing Scheme uses a similar idea.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But construction cost then, as it is today, fluctuates based on economic factors, like labour availability, the price of construction material, global commodities like oil and so on.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In the 1960s and 1970s, construction costs were relatively low, but the turning point came at around 1979.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, Mr Leong presents, selectively, the 1979 data, but does not mention what happens in the next one, two years.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: He did not share this with the House.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In fact, the challenge of sharply fluctuating construction and therefore, HDB prices, according to the AHS, when pegged to construction costs, applies equally to the PSP's Affordable Housing Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In fact, we do not price flats to recover land and construction cost.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We look at the market value of the flat, apply significant market discounts to bring the price down so that there are flats affordable to Singaporeans of different income levels.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And then, we do means testing for explicit grants on top of the market discounts.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This ensures HDB flats remain affordable to a wide range of incomes.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Is this really the kind of Singapore that we want to have?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I have repeatedly spoken at length to this House and also, rebutted Mr Leong's allegations in terms of the statistics not being transparent.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I want to use, perhaps, a Cantonese movie anecdote and I will translate.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: (In Cantonese):   When I speak, you do not listen.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When you understand, you do not do it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When you do it, you do it wrong.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When you do it wrong, you do not admit it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When you admit it, you do not change.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When you change, you do not accept it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: What then do you want me to do? : I have done my best repeatedly to explain to him over and over again, but he still refuses to accept —

speaker: The Chairman
text: Minister Tan, you might want to translate for those who do not understand Cantonese.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Louis Ng, sorry, I know you filed four cuts but we have run out of time.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Can I invite Mr Desmond Choo, if you would like to withdraw your amendment?
